URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS273880171	2020-10-22 18:47:28	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1					United States	US	California	US-CA	Imperial	US-CA-025	BIRDLIFE_26227|US-CA_269	33			Imperial Irrigation District Wetland Project--Niland	L866412	H	33.2118848	-115.5204034	2014-09-27	13:30:00	obsr153343		S19976447	Traveling	Traveling	P22			40	3.219		4	0	G1009643	1	1	1		Observers were Tom Benson, Howard King, Brad Singer, and Matt Grube. We returned to the IID Wetlands after lunch to try a second time for the Yellow-crowned Night-Heron. We were successful in finding it this time, and spent most of our time studying the heron as it perched within the reeds, and later out in the open. Weather was clear with light winds and temps around 93 degrees F.	Continuing second year bird initially found by Matt Gearheart on 23 Sep, and seen again by Guy McCaskie on 25 Sep. While scanning the area where Guy had reported seeing it, I (TAB) noticed a large grayish blob standing in the water within a patch of dry reeds, and I was able to see enough of the head pattern to determine that it was the YCNH. We were able to obtain scope views of the bird, but it was largely obscured by the reeds. After ten or fifteen minutes of these obstructed views, the bird miraculously flew out of the reeds and landed on some matted-down reeds along the east edge of the same pond, allowing unobstructed views for another ten minutes. This was a small, rather stocky heron with long legs (the tail extending to a point just below the ankles while standing, and the tarsi and feet extending well beyond the tail tip in flight). Over all the bird was primarily dark gray. The feathers of the upper parts were dark gray with pale gray edges, creating a neatly scalloped appearance. The under parts were also mostly gray, but with some whitish streaking throughout indicative of retained juvenile plumage. The head pattern was diagnostic, being blackish with a narrow, creamy-white stripe extending from the gape of the bill underneath the eye and widening to its terminus at the nape, and a grayish-yellow forehead that extended posteriorly and became narrower over the crown to its terminus at the nape. The iris was a striking red-orange color, and there was a single white filoplume extending from the hindcrown. The bill was primarily blackish, and noticeably "heavy" and deep. Matt Grube's flight photos showed a mixture of contrasting new and retained remiges, also indicative of a second year bird.

This bar tailed godwit was originally spotted By Naresh Satyan as early as 8/7 then spotted and reported by Larry Schmahl on 8/9.  Apparently it was observed for about 10 minutes along the sand bar before the tide surge this morning with a host of willets and marbled godwits .  We first observed it when it flew to the outer beach.  A large group of birders gathered rather quickly and began observing this bird.  It ran up and down the beach multiple times in a rising tide snagging multiple sand crabs along the way.  This bar tailed godwit was in close proximity to numerous marbled godwits for comparison.  It was slightly smaller than a marbled godwits and a bit larger than the willets.  Overall the bird was lighter buff colored below and its over color was more gray taupe w a cooler vs warmer palette of the marbled godwits.  The barring on its tail was clearly visible  though slight even as it walked down the beach.  When it lifted its wings and took off the extent of the barring was evident on the tail and under the wings. URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS1273309813	2025-06-19 02:33:00.815776	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1					United States	US	California	US-CA	Marin	US-CA-041		32			Shore behind Alta Rock Energy	L16844876	P	37.8661431	-122.4958771	2021-11-08	06:29:00	obsr1418435		S97297878	Traveling	Traveling	P22			15	0.103		1	1		1	1	1			Lifer! This is a continuing bird, originally found this season on 10/13 by Robert T, and very likely the same bird returning to this general area for at least the third year in a row. It was standing in shallow water close to a muddy shoreline along with five other Black-crowned Night-herons and a Great Blue Heron. As I watched, it flew a short distance to a short bare tree. It held its eyelid partly up then closed it completely for a while, but I didn't notice anything really out of the ordinary about it. It appeared to be roughly the same size as the Black-crowned Night-herons, but perhaps it was slightly chunkier (or just more floofed out). Certainly the bill was thicker and pale yellow on the base of the lower mandible. The eye looked large, with a thin, red iris. It had a very distinctive head pattern being mostly black with white horizontal patches under the eyes, and a very thick, prominent, yellow crown-stripe. The back and wings were a slightly blueish gray with thick white stripes bordering thicker dark centers on the scaps, coverts, and what I could see of the flight feathers. The legs were an almost orangish yellow. It did not vocalize while I was there.----I feel like I at least think this, if not actually write it about for the majority of life birds I find these days, but I really needed to see this bird. I suppose there are possibly other hobbies that could possibly instill FOMO more than this one, but I don't know any. And I hate missing out. That's what I did the last time this bird was hanging out here at least between January and February and perhaps for all of fall and winter since someone had put it up on iNaturalist back in September. I kept wanting to make it out here, but never made it happen. This year I was determined not to miss it again, but the first time I came out looking for it I made the mistake of looking where it had been reported in 2019 and winter 2020, which was off by three quarters of a mile from where it is now. Since then, I've only had four chances to go birding this far from home and the first three I spent dipping (grumble grumble) on other rare birds I thought might not stick around as long (Virginia's Warbler, Thick-billed Kingbird, and Gray Catbird). Now that daylight savings time has ended, I have more time in the morning before work to go birding, and this first day of those good circumstances didn't disappoint in the slightest. It took less than a minute to see one Black-crowned Night-heron and only seconds more to find the yellow. It's been over 2.5 years since I saw my first Black-crowned Night-heron that sparked my interest in this obsessive hobby, and it's cousin here is now the 10th heron I've been lucky enough to see.

It was most visible when I leaned over/toward the East railing of the pier, as a branchlet obscured views from further West— I was at at least 3/4 of the way to the end of the structure. Slate gray body, cream-yellow namesake head color, and distinct white bar beneath eyeline.

Other birders arrived while I was there including Curtis Marantz.	A juvenile with brownish gray plumage marked with small white spots and edges. The underparts were whitish with dark brown streaks. The bill was heavy and black (it did show some yellowish at base of lower mandible but none along the cutting edge of the bill). The legs were pale and appeared relatively long (there was no adjacent Black-crowned Night-Heron for direct comparison – they were nearby but when I looked at them for comparison, I only considered the bill shape and covert pattern and forgot about leg length). The coverts had neat white fringes and a smallish white triangular shaped white spot at tip of feather. The primaries were tipped thinly with white. The back was dark grayish brown (overall the feathers looked worn, but some of the mantle feathers were darker and may have been fresh indicating second generation of feathers). The scapulars as well as the head had smaller and more elongated versions of this triangular shaped white spots. A white streak below the eye was evident (Joe Morlan mentioned this on his Monday post to Orange County Birding as possibly a mark for YCNH). The eye color (iris) was orangish and the unfeathered lores were yellowish.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS333311775	2023-12-21 10:27:08.024675	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1					United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059	BIRDLIFE_26213|BIRDLIFE_31214	32			Bolsa Chica--walkbridge/inner bay	L1165694	H	33.6965128	-118.0451372	2015-07-19	06:00:00	obsr353889		S24379397	Traveling	Traveling	P22			120	1.609		1	0		0	1	1		Sunny, winds calm. Walked from PCH lot around tidal basin to check for shorebirds during low tide.	I encountered an unusual night heron on my loop walk. I saw it at about 7:30 am foraging from the riprap lining the south side of the Wintersburg Channel about 25 feet east of the footbridge at the back of the muted tidal pond. The fine white spotting and heavy bill caught my eye so I stopped to observe its behavior and take some photograps. My 1st impression was that this bird was a Yellow-crowned Night Heron. It appeared to have crisp feathers, so likely a bird that recently flegdged. The feathers of the upperparts were a uniform pale gray-brown color with fine triangular white tips to each feather of the wings and back. The secondaries were also finely edged with white. The face, head, and neck were densely covered with narrow white streaks. The eye was red. The legs were yellow and fairly long giving the bird a gangly appearance. The bird had yellow lores. The bill was thick with an all gray upper mandible. The lower mandible was mostly gray at the tip becoming more yellow closer to the base. While watching this bird forage I also saw the long neck characteristic of yellow-crowneds. An adult black-crowned was standing on the riprap some 10 feet away allowing for good comparisons. My presence disturbed the black-crowned sufficiently that it flushed and flew off croaking in protest into the muted tidal pond. The yellow-crowned was aware of my presence but was not the least perturbed. The prior 2 yellow-crowneds that appeared at Bolsa were also not fazed by passersby. I'm not sure if yellow-crowned are approachable by nature or if these particular birds were acclimated to the presence of people while young. A few features of the bird made me wonder whether this was a "pure" yellow-crowned after all.  I had previously observed 2 juvenile yellow-crowneds at Bolsa Chica - the first in the winter of 2012/13 and the second in August 2014. Several features of this bird struck me as different from the previous records. The extent of the yellow in the lower bill and yellow lores struck me as unusual as the previous birds had lower manibles that were mostly gray with the yellow restricted to a thin line running along the bottom from tip to base and grayish lores. The bill on this bird also seemed to me somewhat thinner and more sharply tipped than the prior two. The 2012 & 2014 birds had obviously thick and blunt tipped bills that felt different from this one. Later in comparing my photos of this bird to the prior two birds I noticed that this bird's contact line between the upper and lower mandibles was slightly downcurved near the tip of the bill whereas the prior birds had a straight contact line running the length of the bill. There's been some debate among birders whether this is a "pure" or hybrid bird which goes beyond my abilities and experience as a birder. High tide at 9:32 AM; 2.0 ft Low tide at 2:45 PM--Skipper: Robert Sloan Counters: Jeff Bray, Sally Menzel, Sharon Harrow, Darrell Wilson, Mark Kincheloe,--Chuck Nichols, Sandy Smith, Jan Wilson, and Nancy Kenyon.--Comments: We had perfect weather for our trip; it was comfortably warm and the sky was overcast with no breeze.--There was no glare and the colors of the birds’ plumage stood out well against the mud flats and vegetation along the--shore. For most of the trip, the water was so calm that we were able to enjoy perfect reflections of the shoreline.--We saw several species of raptors: 7 Ospreys, two of which were calling back and forth to each other from across the--channel; a kestrel was perched on the Osprey’s nesting platform by the Back-Bay Science Center; 2 White-tailed Kites--were near each other in a tree; a Northern Harrier was chasing a flock of Willets in flight; and a Red-tailed Hawk was--perched high on the side of a cliff overlooking the bay.--The Least and Western Sandpipers must have arrived recently; they were still in enormous flocks tightly massed--together on the mudflats. When a flock took off in flight, it was like a glimmering cloud. Since the tide was still high,--there weren’t any spacious mud flats from which they could feed. There were lots of Black-bellied Plovers massed on--top of the Santa Ynez Spit as well as on a couple of mud flats and many still had black bellies. Other shorebirds--included Whimbrels, Long-billed Curlews, Marbled Godwits, Short-billed Dowitchers, Spotted Sandpipers, and Willets.--Barn Swallows were swooping overhead catching insects. Western Gulls were all over the place. Large Mullets were--leaping out of the water. Caspian Terns were resting in their usual spot right below the Science Center, their red bills--prominent in the soft lighting. In the little bay past the Caspian Terns, we were thrilled to spot a juvenile Yellow-crowned--Night Heron feeding on crabs at the water’s edge. We sat in the boat watching him for quite a while and he paid no--attention to us. There were a number of Snowy Egrets singly and in groups all the way along. The Black Skimmers were--still inhabiting the upper part of the bay in giant flocks, many on the ground, some flying around and we could hear their--distinctive cry from quite a distance. On the way back, we watched with amusement as a Great Blue Heron stood on--the shore quite close to a fisherman, waiting for a chance to grab his fish when he pulled it out of the water.--Unfortunately we were unable to linger to find out who got the fish.	ID by Jeff Bray

We had average numbers of Black-vented Shearwaters and Pomarine and Parasitic Jaegers, but everything else including terns, alcids, and storm-petrels seemed to be present in below average numbers. The highlight was clearly two different Red-billed Tropicbirds that gave incredible views as they flew past the boat multiple times. Weather was mostly sunny with a few scattered clouds, some fog further offshore, and relatively calm seas and light winds throughout the day.----This checklist covers the area about two miles outside the harbor at the edge of the 100-fathom curve to our traverse through the harbor back to the dock. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended about 1.6 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26' 26" N, 117° 41' 51" W).  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly and stopped only briefly, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  There was a full, low overcast throughout this period, calm conditions, and a temperature of 60° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle on his arrival). This last leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters about 0.85 kilometers west of Dana Point at 33° 27' 27" N, 117° 43' 26" W, along the outer breakwater, and then through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  Even offshore, the depth of the water was less than 25 meters during this leg of the trip, and for much of our time off the breakwater, we were in water no more than 10-meters-deep.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.56 kilometers, which represents an accurate, one-way distance for this leg of the trip, during which we passed by the tip of the breakwater at 2:48 pm, and reached the dock at 3:00 pm.  We saw no pelagic species during this part of the trip, but we did see moderate numbers of all three cormorant species, including three Pelagic Cormorants, and over 100 pelicans.  We saw relatively few gulls and terns, yet the birds seen included at least one Heermann's Gull, two Elegant Terns, small numbers of a variety of shorebirds and herons, including a young Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, and a few land birds.  Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel. Even offshore, the depth of the water was less than 25 meters during this leg of the trip, and for much of our time off the breakwater, we were in water no more than 10-meters-deep.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.56 kilometers, which represents an accurate, one-way distance for this leg of the trip, during which we passed by the tip of the breakwater at 2:48 pm, and reached the dock at 3:00 pm.  We saw no pelagic species during this part of the trip, but we did see moderate numbers of all three cormorant species, including three Pelagic Cormorants, and over 100 pelicans.  We saw relatively few gulls and terns, yet the birds seen included at least one Heermann's Gull, two Elegant Terns, small numbers of a variety of shorebirds and herons, including a young Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, and a few land birds.  Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping along the way, this list is best considered an incomplete one for a superficial search of the harbor channel, outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was clear, but hazy, with a mild (5 knot) breeze from the southeast, and a temperature of 63° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Marantz's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater represented a 1-2 foot swell from the southwest and a choppy to rippled surface.  Data from the nearshore, Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located on inshore waters off San Onofre at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 13½ kilometers south-southeast of the tip of the breakwater, represented a wave height at a constant 2.0 feet [=0.61 meters] with a dominant period from the west-southwest to the south at 13-17 seconds, and an average period ranging 6.9-7.3 seconds; water temperature during this period ranged 61.2-61.3º F (on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  2:35-3:10 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list. Although we saw three Black Oystercatchers, we missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor in recent weeks.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered incomplete. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite three kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 25' 59" N, 117° 42' 35" W), from which we cruised up to the base of the breakwater, and then along and around the tip, before eventually continuing through the harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:34 pm and we reached the dock at 3:47 pm.  This leg of the trip began in waters about 70 meters in depth, but most of our route was in truly shallow waters less than 25-meters deep.  We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, despite seeing large numbers of Heermann's Gulls and moderate numbers of Western Gulls and Elegant Terns.  Also present were large numbers of Brown Pelicans, and moderate numbers of both Double-crested and Brandt's Cormorants, yet we saw only two Pelagic Cormorants.  Once at the breakwater, we saw two each Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Black Oystercatchers, but we failed to see any other shorebirds.  Finally, we added several each Rock Pigeons and American Crows as we cruised through the harbor.  Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 5.28 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance despite the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor.  It was again partly cloudy, with a 20% cover of mid-level clouds just offshore at the beginning of this period transitioning to clear skies overhead but with clouds offshore to the southwest by our return to the dock.  On our arrival at the dock, we noted a mild (10 knot) breeze from the northwest, and an air temperature of 75° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The swell from the west appeared to drop to 1-2 feet, but still with a choppy surface just offshore.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.8-0.9 meters [= 2.6-3.0 feet] with a dominant period of 14-15 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 6.6-8.0 seconds, and water temperature ranging 20.2-20.3º C [ = 68.4-68.5º F] (all data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:15-3:50 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in red, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about two kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26' 23" N, 117° 42' 04" W).  We saw only moderate numbers of gulls and cormorants on the breakwater, but many pelicans.  Although we saw three Black Oystercatchers, we missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor in recent weeks.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 2.59 miles, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  On our departure from the harbor, we had a moderately dense fog that reached the water, calm conditions at the dock but a mild (5+ knot) breeze from the west just offshore, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater were mild, with a 1-2 foot swell from the west and a rippled surface.  7:05-7:25 am.----The track for the day is shown below in red, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen.  We traveled along this path in an out-and-back trip to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop and spent extended periods of time around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll.----<a href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/cmarantz/53903269366/in/dateposted-public/" title="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic (revised) - 20 July 2024"><img src="https://live.staticflickr.com/65535/53903269366_0cccf28c54_o.jpg" alt="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic (revised) - 20 July 2024" /></a>	(we saw a streaky juvenile heron standing along the water on the inside of the breakwater)

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS2369190041	2025-08-14 22:57:38.70729	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				2				Unknown Sex, Immature (2)	United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2024-07-20	15:15:00	obsr237677		S190442942	Traveling	Traveling	P22			35	5.282		37	0	G12776534	1	1	0		This report represents the last in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O'Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite three kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 25' 59" N, 117° 42' 35" W), from which we cruised up to the base of the breakwater, and then along and around the tip, before eventually continuing through the harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:34 pm and we reached the dock at 3:47 pm.  This leg of the trip began in waters about 70 meters in depth, but most of our route was in truly shallow waters less than 25-meters deep.  We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, despite seeing large numbers of Heermann's Gulls and moderate numbers of Western Gulls and Elegant Terns.  Also present were large numbers of Brown Pelicans, and moderate numbers of both Double-crested and Brandt's Cormorants, yet we saw only two Pelagic Cormorants.  Once at the breakwater, we saw two each Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Black Oystercatchers, but we failed to see any other shorebirds.  Finally, we added several each Rock Pigeons and American Crows as we cruised through the harbor.  Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 5.28 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance despite the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor.  It was again partly cloudy, with a 20% cover of mid-level clouds just offshore at the beginning of this period transitioning to clear skies overhead but with clouds offshore to the southwest by our return to the dock.  On our arrival at the dock, we noted a mild (10 knot) breeze from the northwest, and an air temperature of 75° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The swell from the west appeared to drop to 1-2 feet, but still with a choppy surface just offshore.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.8-0.9 meters [= 2.6-3.0 feet] with a dominant period of 14-15 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 6.6-8.0 seconds, and water temperature ranging 20.2-20.3º C [ = 68.4-68.5º F] (all data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:15-3:50 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in red, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen.  We traveled along this path in an out-and-back trip to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop and spent extended periods of time around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll.----<a href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/cmarantz/53903269366/in/dateposted-public/" title="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic (revised) - 20 July 2024"><img src="https://live.staticflickr.com/65535/53903269366_0cccf28c54_o.jpg" alt="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic (revised) - 20 July 2024" /></a>	(we saw as we cruised through the harbor two young night-herons along the waterline on the inside of the breakwater)

This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about two kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26' 23" N, 117° 42' 04" W).  We saw only moderate numbers of gulls and cormorants on the breakwater, but many pelicans.  Although we saw three Black Oystercatchers, we missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor in recent weeks.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 2.59 miles, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  On our departure from the harbor, we had a moderately dense fog that reached the water, calm conditions at the dock but a mild (5+ knot) breeze from the west just offshore, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater were mild, with a 1-2 foot swell from the west and a rippled surface.  7:05-7:25 am.----The track for the day is shown below in red, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite three kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 25' 59" N, 117° 42' 35" W), from which we cruised up to the base of the breakwater, and then along and around the tip, before eventually continuing through the harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:34 pm and we reached the dock at 3:47 pm.  This leg of the trip began in waters about 70 meters in depth, but most of our route was in truly shallow waters less than 25-meters deep.  We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, despite seeing large numbers of Heermann's Gulls and moderate numbers of Western Gulls and Elegant Terns.  Also present were large numbers of Brown Pelicans, and moderate numbers of both Double-crested and Brandt's Cormorants, yet we saw only two Pelagic Cormorants.  Once at the breakwater, we saw two each Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Black Oystercatchers, but we failed to see any other shorebirds.  Finally, we added several each Rock Pigeons and American Crows as we cruised through the harbor.  Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 5.28 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance despite the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor.  It was again partly cloudy, with a 20% cover of mid-level clouds just offshore at the beginning of this period transitioning to clear skies overhead but with clouds offshore to the southwest by our return to the dock.  On our arrival at the dock, we noted a mild (10 knot) breeze from the northwest, and an air temperature of 75° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The swell from the west appeared to drop to 1-2 feet, but still with a choppy surface just offshore. URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS2369263080	2025-08-14 22:55:59.444583	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				2				Unknown Sex, Immature (2)	United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2024-07-20	15:15:00	obsr2216543		S190447333	Traveling	Traveling	P22			35	5.282		37	0	G12776534	1	1	0		This report represents the last in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O'Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite three kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 25' 59" N, 117° 42' 35" W), from which we cruised up to the base of the breakwater, and then along and around the tip, before eventually continuing through the harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:34 pm and we reached the dock at 3:47 pm.  This leg of the trip began in waters about 70 meters in depth, but most of our route was in truly shallow waters less than 25-meters deep.  We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, despite seeing large numbers of Heermann's Gulls and moderate numbers of Western Gulls and Elegant Terns.  Also present were large numbers of Brown Pelicans, and moderate numbers of both Double-crested and Brandt's Cormorants, yet we saw only two Pelagic Cormorants.  Once at the breakwater, we saw two each Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Black Oystercatchers, but we failed to see any other shorebirds.  Finally, we added several each Rock Pigeons and American Crows as we cruised through the harbor.  Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 5.28 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance despite the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor.  It was again partly cloudy, with a 20% cover of mid-level clouds just offshore at the beginning of this period transitioning to clear skies overhead but with clouds offshore to the southwest by our return to the dock.  On our arrival at the dock, we noted a mild (10 knot) breeze from the northwest, and an air temperature of 75° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The swell from the west appeared to drop to 1-2 feet, but still with a choppy surface just offshore.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.8-0.9 meters [= 2.6-3.0 feet] with a dominant period of 14-15 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 6.6-8.0 seconds, and water temperature ranging 20.2-20.3º C [ = 68.4-68.5º F] (all data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:15-3:50 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in red, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:05 am, and left the dock at 7:07 am. We saw only moderate numbers of gulls and cormorants on the breakwater, but many pelicans.  Although we saw three Black Oystercatchers, we missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor in recent weeks.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered incomplete. On our departure from the harbor, we had a moderately dense fog that reached the water, calm conditions at the dock but a mild (5+ knot) breeze from the west just offshore, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle). Once at the breakwater, we saw two each Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Black Oystercatchers, but we failed to see any other shorebirds.  Finally, we added several each Rock Pigeons and American Crows as we cruised through the harbor.  Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 5.28 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance despite the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor.  It was again partly cloudy, with a 20% cover of mid-level clouds just offshore at the beginning of this period transitioning to clear skies overhead but with clouds offshore to the southwest by our return to the dock.  On our arrival at the dock, we noted a mild (10 knot) breeze from the northwest, and an air temperature of 75° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The swell from the west appeared to drop to 1-2 feet, but still with a choppy surface just offshore. Once at the breakwater, we saw two each Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Black Oystercatchers, but we failed to see any other shorebirds.  Finally, we added several each Rock Pigeons and American Crows as we cruised through the harbor.  Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 5.28 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance despite the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor.  It was again partly cloudy, with a 20% cover of mid-level clouds just offshore at the beginning of this period transitioning to clear skies overhead but with clouds offshore to the southwest by our return to the dock.  On our arrival at the dock, we noted a mild (10 knot) breeze from the northwest, and an air temperature of 75° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The swell from the west appeared to drop to 1-2 feet, but still with a choppy surface just offshore.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.8-0.9 meters [= 2.6-3.0 feet] with a dominant period of 14-15 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 6.6-8.0 seconds, and water temperature ranging 20.2-20.3º C [ = 68.4-68.5º F] (all data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:15-3:50 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in red, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite three kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 25' 59" N, 117° 42' 35" W), from which we cruised up to the base of the breakwater, and then along and around the tip, before eventually continuing through the harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:34 pm and we reached the dock at 3:47 pm.  This leg of the trip began in waters about 70 meters in depth, but most of our route was in truly shallow waters less than 25-meters deep.  We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, despite seeing large numbers of Heermann's Gulls and moderate numbers of Western Gulls and Elegant Terns.  Also present were large numbers of Brown Pelicans, and moderate numbers of both Double-crested and Brandt's Cormorants, yet we saw only two Pelagic Cormorants.  Once at the breakwater, we saw two each Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Black Oystercatchers, but we failed to see any other shorebirds.  Finally, we added several each Rock Pigeons and American Crows as we cruised through the harbor.  Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 5.28 kilometers, which should represent an accurate, one-way distance despite the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor.  It was again partly cloudy, with a 20% cover of mid-level clouds just offshore at the beginning of this period transitioning to clear skies overhead but with clouds offshore to the southwest by our return to the dock.  On our arrival at the dock, we noted a mild (10 knot) breeze from the northwest, and an air temperature of 75° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The swell from the west appeared to drop to 1-2 feet, but still with a choppy surface just offshore. URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS2448404931	2026-05-26 20:09:40.18727	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				2				Unknown Sex, Immature (2)	United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2024-08-24	07:10:00	obsr2076639		S194493484	Traveling	Traveling	P22			25	3.866		51	0	G12940088	1	1	0		This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am.  We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W).  We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants.  We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer.  We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow.  Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am.  We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W).  We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants.  We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer.  We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow.  Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am.  We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W).  We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants.  We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer.  We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow.  Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen.  We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am. This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W).  We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants. Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 11¾ kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 11-13 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period of 6.3-6.7 seconds, and water temperature ranging 23.0-23.1° C [ = 73.4-73.6° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:40-4:00 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen.  We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll. URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS2470132404	2026-05-26 20:09:40.172743	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				2				Unknown Sex, Immature (2)	United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2024-08-24	07:10:00	obsr293612		S195529866	Traveling	Traveling	P22			25	3.866		51	0	G12940088	1	1	0		This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am.  We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W).  We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants.  We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer.  We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow.  Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen.  We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll.  After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----<a href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/cmarantz/53962448998/in/dateposted-public/" title="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic - 24 August 2024"><img src="https://live.staticflickr.com/65535/53962448998_f098990bcd_o.jpg" alt="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic - 24 August 2024" /></a>	(we saw on our departure from the harbor two night herons, a subadult that was probably a bit older than one-year of age, and what was likely a juvenile or first-year bird)

We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am.  We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W).  We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants.  We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer.  We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow.  Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite two kilometers almost due south of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 14” N, 117° 41’ 48” W), from which we cruised around the tip of the breakwater, and through the main harbor channel to the Ocean Institute dock.  We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm.  This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout.  We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants.  We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether.  Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds.  Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe.  Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor.  It was again clear but a bit hazy, with a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the west, and an air temperature of 74° F on our return to the dock (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The swell from the west appeared to drop to about 2 feet, but still with a mixed component, and a rippled to choppy surface just offshore.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 11¾ kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 11-13 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period of 6.3-6.7 seconds, and water temperature ranging 23.0-23.1° C [ = 73.4-73.6° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:40-4:00 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am.  We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W).  We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants.  We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer.  We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow.  Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. Our ninth and last leg of the trip began on the inshore waters when we reached the shelf not quite two kilometers almost due south of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 14” N, 117° 41’ 48” W), from which we cruised around the tip of the breakwater, and through the main harbor channel to the Ocean Institute dock.  We passed the tip of the breakwater at 3:46 pm and we reached the dock at 4:00 pm.  This leg of the trip began in waters about 20 meters in depth and remained in truly shallow waters throughout.  We saw no truly pelagic species during this period, though we saw good numbers of both Heermann's and Western Gulls, Brown Pelicans, and Double-crested Cormorants.  We saw only five Brandt's Cormorants and we missed Pelagic Cormorant altogether.  Once inside the harbor, some aboard saw at least one Yellow-crowned Night Heron, a Snowy Egret, and several Great Blue Herons, and we again saw the Black Oystercatcher family, but we saw no other shorebirds.  Finally, while cruising through the harbor to the dock, we added a Western Grebe, a few Caspian Terns, some Rock Pigeons, a couple of American Crows, and a Black Phoebe.  Given that we cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, this list is probably best considered an incomplete one of the birds that were likely present.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.2 kilometers, which we adjusted to 3.8 kilometers to better reflect our one-way distance given the angles in our track around the breakwater and through the harbor.  It was again clear but a bit hazy, with a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the west, and an air temperature of 74° F on our return to the dock (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The swell from the west appeared to drop to about 2 feet, but still with a mixed component, and a rippled to choppy surface just offshore.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 11¾ kilometers south-southeast of where we began this leg of the trip just off Dana Point, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 11-13 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period of 6.3-6.7 seconds, and water temperature ranging 23.0-23.1° C [ = 73.4-73.6° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:40-4:00 pm.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen.  We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll.  After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----<a href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/cmarantz/53962448998/in/dateposted-public/" title="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic - 24 August 2024"><img src="https://live.staticflickr.com/65535/53962448998_f098990bcd_o.jpg" alt="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic - 24 August 2024" /></a>	(Marantz missed a juvenile night heron that was seen by Benson and others along the inner edge of the breakwater)

We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am.  We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W).  We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants.  We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer.  We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow.  Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen. URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS2430296662	2026-05-26 20:09:40.470995	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				2				Unknown Sex, Immature (2)	United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2024-08-24	07:10:00	obsr551001		S193613903	Traveling	Traveling	P22			25	3.866		51	0	G12940088	1	1	0		This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for a pelagic birding trip from the Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society, with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brad Singer, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am.  We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W).  We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants.  We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer.  We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow.  Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen.  We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll.  After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----<a href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/cmarantz/53962448998/in/dateposted-public/" title="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic - 24 August 2024"><img src="https://live.staticflickr.com/65535/53962448998_f098990bcd_o.jpg" alt="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic - 24 August 2024" /></a>	(we saw on our departure from the harbor two night herons, a subadult that was probably a bit older than one-year of age, and what was likely a juvenile or first-year bird)

We began our day at the Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:08 am, and left the dock at 7:11 am.  We then passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:30 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended a short distance offshore, about 1.7 kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 23” N, 117° 41’ 49” W).  We saw moderate numbers of gulls and pelicans on the breakwater, but relatively few cormorants.  We managed to find the continuing family of Black Oystercatchers on the breakwater, but again missed a white-bellied oystercatcher that had been seen around the harbor this summer.  We also saw a pair of Mallards, two Yellow-crowned Night Herons, one each Snowy Egret and Great Blue Heron, several each Caspian Terns and Barn Swallows (one of which followed us offshore a short distance), and an American Crow.  Marantz also heard what sounded like two Swinhoe's White-eyes calling shortly after we departed the dock.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly, stopping only briefly to check on the oystercatchers, this list is best considered incomplete.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.94 kilometers, from which we adjusted our distance to 3½ kilometers to better represent the one-way distance for our trip through the harbor and just offshore.  On our departure from the harbor, we encountered partly cloudy skies, with a 10% cover of mid-level clouds to the west and southwest, calm conditions, and a temperature of 64° F when we arrived at the Ocean Institute (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  The seas just off the breakwater were a bit choppy, with a three-foot, short-period swell from the west, combined with a two-foot swell from the southwest, and a rippled surface.  Weather data from the Green Beach Offshore waverider buoy, located at 33° 20’ 11” N, 117° 39’ 31” W, and thus about 12 kilometers south-southeast of where we ended this leg of the trip just off the Dana Point breakwater, represented a wave height ranging 0.7-0.8 meters [= 2.3-2.6 feet] with a dominant period of 14 seconds from the south-southwest, an average period ranging 5.5-5.6 seconds, and water temperature steady at 22.5° C [= 72.5° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  7:10-7:35 am.----The track for the day is shown below in green, with the yellow pins denoting the locations where we began each new list and the cyan pins the locations of the more interesting species seen.  We traveled along this path out to Crespi Knoll, over which we took a narrowly counterclockwise loop, spending time both on our way south and again on our way back north around a slick of fish oil and popcorn that we put out midway down the knoll.  After leaving Crespi Knoll, we continued to the northwest toward Catalina Island, before returning across the 279-fathom Bank, and eventually back to Dana Point.----<a href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/cmarantz/53962448998/in/dateposted-public/" title="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic - 24 August 2024"><img src="https://live.staticflickr.com/65535/53962448998_f098990bcd_o.jpg" alt="GPS track - Dana Point pelagic - 24 August 2024" /></a>	(we saw on our departure from the harbor two night herons, a subadult that was probably a bit older than one-year of age, and what was likely a juvenile or first-year bird)

So we instead headed west, along the lee of Catalina island to the western San Pedro channel almost to the 270 bank, where we found very large flocks of feeding Pink-footed Shearwaters and other birds with dolphins and a few whales. After spending about an hour here, we returned along the mid-channel drop off all the way back to Newport Harbor.----Seas were bumpy with 2-3 ft swells and large wind waves south of Catalina island, but pretty calm and comfortable in the San Pedro channel east of the island.----Marine mammals included several pods of common dolphins, a small mixed pod of Risso's and Bottlenose dolphins, two humpback whales, one fin whale, California sea lions, and a distant elephant seal seen by the captain only.----This leg from the dock by the Balboa island ferry to the mouth of Newport Harbor and about 1-2 miles outside the harbor.

We departed the dock at 0715, then cruised slowly along the outer jetty while searching for birds, then turned more or less southwest after exiting the harbor. We headed directly toward the 279 Bank, but finding few birds there, quickly passed over and continued southwest to the north end of Crespi Knoll. We travelled over the high point of the sea mount and continued toward the north end, but finding relatively few birds, turned east-northeast toward Laguna Beach. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602.
