URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS2564721494	2026-05-26 20:07:44.612357	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1					United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2024-10-19	07:15:00	obsr196748		S200315895	Traveling	Traveling	P22			20	3.945		33	1	G13268090	0	1	0		Sea & Sage Audubon held their annual fall pelagic trip on Oct 19 aboard the Ocean Institute's R/V Sea Explorer with Brittany Loust as captain and Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, and Brittany O'Connor as co-leaders. We departed the dock at 0715, then cruised slowly along the outer jetty while searching for birds, then turned more or less southwest after exiting the harbor. We headed directly toward the 279 Bank, but finding few birds there, quickly passed over and continued southwest to the north end of Crespi Knoll. Upon reaching Crespi Knoll, we turned south and made counterclockwise, U-shaped path around the perimeter of the knoll, stopping for birds as necessary, then continuing north-northwest toward the south end of Lausen Sea Mount. We travelled over the high point of the sea mount and continued toward the north end, but finding relatively few birds, turned east-northeast toward Laguna Beach. We followed this course until we reached the escarpment, then followed the escarpment southeast back to Dana Point. As we were nearing the harbor, we noticed a large feeding frenzy over the escarpment southwest of Dana Point, so we spent the remaining time of our trip working the shearwater rafts in this area before eventually returning to the harbor and reaching the dock at 1602. Seas were generally calm all day, with light winds (&lt;10 kts), sunny skies, and temperatures mostly in the 60s (degrees F). This checklist covers our morning transit through the harbor and the inshore waters between the harbor mouth and the escarpment.

On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at 4:50 pm, and then along the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters about 1¾ kilometers southwest of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 36” N, 117° 42’ 20” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 5:02 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered to represent an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw many more birds than we had on our morning departure, with many more Heermann’s and Western Gulls, more pelicans, and many more cormorants, including good numbers of Brandt’s Cormorant, which we all but missed on our morning departure.  We again saw a single oystercatcher sleeping on the breakwater, but also what appeared to be three Spotted Sandpipers, one each of Snowy Egret and Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, several pigeons, and a dozen Barn Swallows.  Also present when we disembarked was an Osprey eating a fish atop the mast of a ship at the dock.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.08 kilometers, which was close to eBird’s adjustment of Benson’s track at 4.16 kilometers.  We noted on our arrival at the dock, clear skies, a mild (10 knot) breeze from the west, and a rather warm 79° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater, waves of two feet from the northwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Weather conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about 2½ kilometers east of where this leg of the trip began just off the breakwater, represented a wave height dropping from 0.9 meters to 0.8 meters [= 3.0 feet and 2.6 feet, respectively], with a dominant period from the southwest to the south-southwest of 15-17 seconds and an average period of 7.8-8.6 seconds, and water temperature dropping from 22.9º C to 22.2º C [= 73.2º F and 72.0º F, respectively], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website.  4:45-5:05 pm.

On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at 4:50 pm, and then along the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters about 1¾ kilometers southwest of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 36” N, 117° 42’ 20” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 5:02 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered to represent an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw many more birds than we had on our morning departure, with many more Heermann’s and Western Gulls, more pelicans, and many more cormorants, including good numbers of Brandt’s Cormorant, which we all but missed on our morning departure.  We again saw a single oystercatcher sleeping on the breakwater, but also what appeared to be three Spotted Sandpipers, one each of Snowy Egret and Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, several pigeons, and a dozen Barn Swallows.  Also present when we disembarked was an Osprey eating a fish atop the mast of a ship at the dock.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.08 kilometers, which was close to eBird’s adjustment of Benson’s track at 4.16 kilometers.  We noted on our arrival at the dock, clear skies, a mild (10 knot) breeze from the west, and a rather warm 79° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater, waves of two feet from the northwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Weather conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about 2½ kilometers east of where this leg of the trip began just off the breakwater, represented a wave height dropping from 0.9 meters to 0.8 meters [= 3.0 feet and 2.6 feet, respectively], with a dominant period from the southwest to the south-southwest of 15-17 seconds and an average period of 7.8-8.6 seconds, and water temperature dropping from 22.9º C to 22.2º C [= 73.2º F and 72.0º F, respectively], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website.  4:45-5:05 pm.

On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at 4:50 pm, and then along the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters about 1¾ kilometers southwest of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 36” N, 117° 42’ 20” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 5:02 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered to represent an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit. The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.08 kilometers, which was close to eBird’s adjustment of Benson’s track at 4.16 kilometers.  We noted on our arrival at the dock, clear skies, a mild (10 knot) breeze from the west, and a rather warm 79° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater, waves of two feet from the northwest, and a rippled to choppy surface. Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered to represent an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit. We noted on our arrival at the dock, clear skies, a mild (10 knot) breeze from the west, and a rather warm 79° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater, waves of two feet from the northwest, and a rippled to choppy surface. URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS3538665797	2025-09-12 20:03:23.576962	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1					United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2025-08-30	16:43:00	obsr280719		S272077431	Traveling	Traveling	P22			19	4.162		37	1	G15519715	1	1	0		This report represents the tenth and last in a set of ten lists for a pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and waters of the Catalina Channel toward the southeastern tip of Catalina Island sponsored by the San Bernardino Valley Audubon Society with Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, Brad Singer, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Jack Parker as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of Ocean Institute.  On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at 4:50 pm, and then along the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters about 1¾ kilometers southwest of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 36” N, 117° 42’ 20” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 5:02 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered to represent an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw many more birds than we had on our morning departure, with many more Heermann’s and Western Gulls, more pelicans, and many more cormorants, including good numbers of Brandt’s Cormorant, which we all but missed on our morning departure.  We again saw a single oystercatcher sleeping on the breakwater, but also what appeared to be three Spotted Sandpipers, one each of Snowy Egret and Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, several pigeons, and a dozen Barn Swallows.  Also present when we disembarked was an Osprey eating a fish atop the mast of a ship at the dock.  The eBird app on Marantz’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.08 kilometers, which was close to eBird’s adjustment of Benson’s track at 4.16 kilometers.  We noted on our arrival at the dock, clear skies, a mild (10 knot) breeze from the west, and a rather warm 79° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater, waves of two feet from the northwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Weather conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about 2½ kilometers east of where this leg of the trip began just off the breakwater, represented a wave height dropping from 0.9 meters to 0.8 meters [= 3.0 feet and 2.6 feet, respectively], with a dominant period from the southwest to the south-southwest of 15-17 seconds and an average period of 7.8-8.6 seconds, and water temperature dropping from 22.9º C to 22.2º C [= 73.2º F and 72.0º F, respectively], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website.  4:45-5:05 pm.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS3676027235	2025-10-19 19:42:56.693429	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				2				Unknown Sex, Juvenile (1); Unknown Sex and Age (1)	United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2025-10-04	15:25:00	obsr290306		S280412047	Traveling	Traveling	P22			20	3.261		29	0	G15706166	0	1	0		This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a &lt;5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.	(Marantz noted that one of the two night-herons seen as we cruised through the harbor was a juvenile, but did not see the other)

Then tried the original south side. Nothing. Then again on the north side— it emerged! I hollered to Jill and Jason who were facing south and they came over and we collectively rejoiced. Bird was lost again as I was leaving, I hustled away but soon I became adjacent to the opening of the mini side ravine on rabbit island halfway along the perpendicular path and I saw the heron working the stream there just as Edana arrived from the opposite direction. This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a &lt;5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface. Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a &lt;5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.	(Marantz noted that one of the two night-herons seen as we cruised through the harbor was a juvenile, but did not see the other)

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS3672558531	2025-10-18 18:34:17.712642	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				2				Unknown Sex and Age (1); Unknown Sex, Juvenile (1)	United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2025-10-04	15:25:00	obsr754941		S280194287	Traveling	Traveling	P22			20	3.261		29	0	G15706166	0	1	0		This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a &lt;5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.	(Marantz noted that one of the two night-herons seen as we cruised through the harbor was a juvenile, but did not see the other)

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS3672534195	2025-10-18 18:22:33.578374	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				2				Unknown Sex, Juvenile (1); Unknown Sex and Age (1)	United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2025-10-04	15:25:00	obsr353889		S280192386	Traveling	Traveling	P22			20	3.261		29	0	G15706166	0	1	0		This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a &lt;5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.	(Marantz noted that one of the two night-herons seen as we cruised through the harbor was a juvenile, but did not see the other)

This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a &lt;5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm. URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS3672164125	2025-10-18 18:19:45.182174	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				2				Unknown Sex and Age (1); Unknown Sex, Juvenile (1)	United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2025-10-04	15:25:00	obsr158843		S280167314	Traveling	Traveling	P22			20	3.261		29	0	G15706166	0	1	0		This report represents the ninth and last in a set of nine lists for the fall pelagic trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll and the waters of the Catalina Channel north to the Lausen Sea Mount, from which we returned to Dana Point.  This trip, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, had as the leaders Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Doug Lithgow as our chummer, and our captain Jack Parker on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  The final leg of the trip took us from the inshore waters, beginning about two kilometers southwest of the tip of the outer breakwater (33° 26’ 30” N, 117° 42’ 21” W), through the Dana Point Harbor to the Ocean Institute dock.  We were in shallow water throughout this leg, which began in only 21 meters of water.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 3.26 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system to reflect our one-way distance.  We passed by the outer breakwater at 3:33 pm, and we reached the dock at 3:43 pm, following a nonstop trip through the harbor.  We managed to get our best views of phalaropes for the day just off the breakwater, and during our trip through the harbor, Marantz counted 110 Brown Pelicans and moderate numbers of both Brandt’s and Double-crested Cormorants, but some aboard saw the only Pelagic Cormorant of the day.  We also saw two-each of both Snowy Egrets and Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, and one each of both Great Egret and Great Blue Heron.  Benson also saw two pigeons and a kingfisher, and we saw at least three crows.  Although we recorded seeing five Royal Terns around the harbor, neither Benson nor Marantz included any of the many Heermann’s and Western Gulls on their lists, so we have included both on the list only as “present.”  We cruised relatively rapidly through the harbor without stopping, which when combined with our failure to record numbers for the gulls is indicative of an incomplete list based on a superficial search of the harbor channel, the outer and inner breakwaters, and the shoreline of the island bordering the main harbor channel.  It was essentially clear, but with a &lt;5% cover of mid-level clouds inland, a mild to moderate (10 knot) breeze from the west on our arrival at the dock, and a temperature of 73° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson's vehicle).  Also noted just offshore was a swell of 2-3 feet from the southwest, and a rippled to choppy surface.  Conditions at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, and thus about 2½ kilometers east of where we began the last leg of the trip, represented a wave height a constant 0.6 meters [= 2.0 feet] with a dominant period from the southwest of 11-14 seconds, an average period ranging 6.1-6.5 seconds, and water temperature ranging 19.3-19.4° C [= 66.7-66.9° F] (data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data).  3:25-3:45 pm.	(Marantz noted that one of the two night-herons seen as we cruised through the harbor was a juvenile, but did not see the other)

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS4881780203	2026-10-01 00:03:41.342144	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				3				Unknown Sex, Adult (1); Unknown Sex, Juvenile (2)	United States	US	California	US-CA	Orange	US-CA-059					Dana Point Harbor	L500764	H	33.4598020	-117.6989365	2026-08-29	07:10:00	obsr158843		S393669705	Traveling	Traveling	P22			30	3.965		47	0	G18294912	1	1	0		This report represents the first in a set of nine lists for the summer pelagic birding trip from Dana Point Harbor out to Crespi Knoll, the Lausen Seamount, and waters of the Catalina Channel, sponsored by the Sea and Sage Audubon Society, with Jon Dunn, Tom Benson, Curtis Marantz, Brittany O’Connor, and Robert McNab as leaders, and with Brittany Loust as our captain on the R/V Sea Explorer out of the Ocean Institute.  We began our day at Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:10 am, and left the dock at 7:16 am.  We passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:33 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended on the inshore waters about 2¼ kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 08” N, 117° 41’ 58” W).  Our trip through the harbor was a relatively direct one, apart from a stop to check out the long-staying bird that has been identified as an American Oystercatcher together with a Black Oystercatcher on the rocks along the western shore of the island, but we also did our best to check the birds on the breakwater, where we found moderate to large numbers of gulls, pelicans, and cormorants. On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at about 4:00 pm, and then through the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters at a depth of about 30 meters approximately 1¾ kilometers essentially due south of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 39” N, 117° 43’ 06” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 4:11 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw good numbers of both Heermann’s and Western Gulls, but only one Elegant Tern, many cormorants and pelicans, along with a Black Oystercatcher, two Spotted Sandpipers, six Snowy Egrets and an adult Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, many pigeons, a Eurasian Collared-Dove, and an American Crow, along with five Mallards and an Osprey, the latter perched in a eucalyptus tree on the island.  Benson also recorded two each Red-necked Phalaropes and Black-vented Shearwaters just off the harbor.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.4 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system, indicating no backtracking along our one-way trip.  It was mostly clear, with a &lt;5% cover of high, thin clouds, a swell from the west to the southwest of 2-3 feet, and a rippled surface offshore, and a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the southwest, and a temperature of 84° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle). We began our day at Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:10 am, and left the dock at 7:16 am.  We passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:33 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended on the inshore waters about 2¼ kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 08” N, 117° 41’ 58” W).  Our trip through the harbor was a relatively direct one, apart from a stop to check out the long-staying bird that has been identified as an American Oystercatcher together with a Black Oystercatcher on the rocks along the western shore of the island, but we also did our best to check the birds on the breakwater, where we found moderate to large numbers of gulls, pelicans, and cormorants. The Black-vented Shearwaters included on this list were noted just before we ended the list, but barely inside the outer buoy.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.12 kilometers, which was converted by the eBird system to a one-way distance of 3.97 kilometers for our trip through the harbor and just offshore (compensating for the loop we made in the channel to check out the oystercatchers).  On our departure from the harbor this morning, we had partly cloudy skies, with a 10-20% cover of high, thin clouds, humid and calm conditions, and a rather balmy temperature of 75° F on our arrival at the port (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater a swell of three feet from the southwest and a rippled surface. We nevertheless saw good numbers of both Heermann’s and Western Gulls, but only one Elegant Tern, many cormorants and pelicans, along with a Black Oystercatcher, two Spotted Sandpipers, six Snowy Egrets and an adult Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, many pigeons, a Eurasian Collared-Dove, and an American Crow, along with five Mallards and an Osprey, the latter perched in a eucalyptus tree on the island.  Benson also recorded two each Red-necked Phalaropes and Black-vented Shearwaters just off the harbor.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.4 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system, indicating no backtracking along our one-way trip.  It was mostly clear, with a &lt;5% cover of high, thin clouds, a swell from the west to the southwest of 2-3 feet, and a rippled surface offshore, and a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the southwest, and a temperature of 84° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle). We began our day at Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:10 am, and left the dock at 7:16 am.  We passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:33 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended on the inshore waters about 2¼ kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 08” N, 117° 41’ 58” W).  Our trip through the harbor was a relatively direct one, apart from a stop to check out the long-staying bird that has been identified as an American Oystercatcher together with a Black Oystercatcher on the rocks along the western shore of the island, but we also did our best to check the birds on the breakwater, where we found moderate to large numbers of gulls, pelicans, and cormorants.  Also seen during this period were a couple of Mallards, a Spotted Sandpiper, a Royal Tern, three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, a Great Blue Heron, two Snowy Egrets, and the usual small numbers of pigeons, crows, and Barn Swallows, along with some unseen Swinhoe’s White-Eyes and a hummingbird that were calling from trees on the island.  The Black-vented Shearwaters included on this list were noted just before we ended the list, but barely inside the outer buoy.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.12 kilometers, which was converted by the eBird system to a one-way distance of 3.97 kilometers for our trip through the harbor and just offshore (compensating for the loop we made in the channel to check out the oystercatchers).  On our departure from the harbor this morning, we had partly cloudy skies, with a 10-20% cover of high, thin clouds, humid and calm conditions, and a rather balmy temperature of 75° F on our arrival at the port (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater a swell of three feet from the southwest and a rippled surface.  Conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about two kilometers northeast of where we ended this leg of the trip, represented a wave height of 1.2-1.4 meters [= 3.9-4.6 feet], with a dominant period from the south-southwest of 18 seconds and an average period ranging 10.1-11.7 seconds, and unusually warm water, given a temperature of 25.7° C [= 78.3° F], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data.  7:10-7:40 am. We began our day at Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:10 am, and left the dock at 7:16 am.  We passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:33 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended on the inshore waters about 2¼ kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 08” N, 117° 41’ 58” W).  Our trip through the harbor was a relatively direct one, apart from a stop to check out the long-staying bird that has been identified as an American Oystercatcher together with a Black Oystercatcher on the rocks along the western shore of the island, but we also did our best to check the birds on the breakwater, where we found moderate to large numbers of gulls, pelicans, and cormorants.  Also seen during this period were a couple of Mallards, a Spotted Sandpiper, a Royal Tern, three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, a Great Blue Heron, two Snowy Egrets, and the usual small numbers of pigeons, crows, and Barn Swallows, along with some unseen Swinhoe’s White-Eyes and a hummingbird that were calling from trees on the island.  The Black-vented Shearwaters included on this list were noted just before we ended the list, but barely inside the outer buoy.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.12 kilometers, which was converted by the eBird system to a one-way distance of 3.97 kilometers for our trip through the harbor and just offshore (compensating for the loop we made in the channel to check out the oystercatchers).  On our departure from the harbor this morning, we had partly cloudy skies, with a 10-20% cover of high, thin clouds, humid and calm conditions, and a rather balmy temperature of 75° F on our arrival at the port (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater a swell of three feet from the southwest and a rippled surface.  Conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about two kilometers northeast of where we ended this leg of the trip, represented a wave height of 1.2-1.4 meters [= 3.9-4.6 feet], with a dominant period from the south-southwest of 18 seconds and an average period ranging 10.1-11.7 seconds, and unusually warm water, given a temperature of 25.7° C [= 78.3° F], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data.  7:10-7:40 am. Our trip through the harbor was a relatively direct one, apart from a stop to check out the long-staying bird that has been identified as an American Oystercatcher together with a Black Oystercatcher on the rocks along the western shore of the island, but we also did our best to check the birds on the breakwater, where we found moderate to large numbers of gulls, pelicans, and cormorants. The Black-vented Shearwaters included on this list were noted just before we ended the list, but barely inside the outer buoy.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.12 kilometers, which was converted by the eBird system to a one-way distance of 3.97 kilometers for our trip through the harbor and just offshore (compensating for the loop we made in the channel to check out the oystercatchers). We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater a swell of three feet from the southwest and a rippled surface. On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at about 4:00 pm, and then through the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters at a depth of about 30 meters approximately 1¾ kilometers essentially due south of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 39” N, 117° 43’ 06” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 4:11 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw good numbers of both Heermann’s and Western Gulls, but only one Elegant Tern, many cormorants and pelicans, along with a Black Oystercatcher, two Spotted Sandpipers, six Snowy Egrets and an adult Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, many pigeons, a Eurasian Collared-Dove, and an American Crow, along with five Mallards and an Osprey, the latter perched in a eucalyptus tree on the island.  Benson also recorded two each Red-necked Phalaropes and Black-vented Shearwaters just off the harbor.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.4 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system, indicating no backtracking along our one-way trip.  It was mostly clear, with a &lt;5% cover of high, thin clouds, a swell from the west to the southwest of 2-3 feet, and a rippled surface offshore, and a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the southwest, and a temperature of 84° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle). We began our day at Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:10 am, and left the dock at 7:16 am.  We passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:33 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended on the inshore waters about 2¼ kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 08” N, 117° 41’ 58” W).  Our trip through the harbor was a relatively direct one, apart from a stop to check out the long-staying bird that has been identified as an American Oystercatcher together with a Black Oystercatcher on the rocks along the western shore of the island, but we also did our best to check the birds on the breakwater, where we found moderate to large numbers of gulls, pelicans, and cormorants.  Also seen during this period were a couple of Mallards, a Spotted Sandpiper, a Royal Tern, three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, a Great Blue Heron, two Snowy Egrets, and the usual small numbers of pigeons, crows, and Barn Swallows, along with some unseen Swinhoe’s White-Eyes and a hummingbird that were calling from trees on the island.  The Black-vented Shearwaters included on this list were noted just before we ended the list, but barely inside the outer buoy.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.12 kilometers, which was converted by the eBird system to a one-way distance of 3.97 kilometers for our trip through the harbor and just offshore (compensating for the loop we made in the channel to check out the oystercatchers).  On our departure from the harbor this morning, we had partly cloudy skies, with a 10-20% cover of high, thin clouds, humid and calm conditions, and a rather balmy temperature of 75° F on our arrival at the port (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater a swell of three feet from the southwest and a rippled surface.  Conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about two kilometers northeast of where we ended this leg of the trip, represented a wave height of 1.2-1.4 meters [= 3.9-4.6 feet], with a dominant period from the south-southwest of 18 seconds and an average period ranging 10.1-11.7 seconds, and unusually warm water, given a temperature of 25.7° C [= 78.3° F], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data.  7:10-7:40 am. We began our day at Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:10 am, and left the dock at 7:16 am.  We passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:33 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended on the inshore waters about 2¼ kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 08” N, 117° 41’ 58” W).  Our trip through the harbor was a relatively direct one, apart from a stop to check out the long-staying bird that has been identified as an American Oystercatcher together with a Black Oystercatcher on the rocks along the western shore of the island, but we also did our best to check the birds on the breakwater, where we found moderate to large numbers of gulls, pelicans, and cormorants.  Also seen during this period were a couple of Mallards, a Spotted Sandpiper, a Royal Tern, three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, a Great Blue Heron, two Snowy Egrets, and the usual small numbers of pigeons, crows, and Barn Swallows, along with some unseen Swinhoe’s White-Eyes and a hummingbird that were calling from trees on the island.  The Black-vented Shearwaters included on this list were noted just before we ended the list, but barely inside the outer buoy.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.12 kilometers, which was converted by the eBird system to a one-way distance of 3.97 kilometers for our trip through the harbor and just offshore (compensating for the loop we made in the channel to check out the oystercatchers). We began our day at Dana Point Harbor at the dock for the Ocean Institute, where we arrived at 6:30 am, did an orientation, boarded the boat at 7:10 am, and left the dock at 7:16 am.  We passed slowly through the main harbor channel, checking the birds on the outer breakwater, along the shore of the island, and then the inner breakwater, before we passed through the harbor mouth at 7:33 am and continued offshore.  This list began when we boarded the boat and ended on the inshore waters about 2¼ kilometers south-southwest of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 08” N, 117° 41’ 58” W).  Our trip through the harbor was a relatively direct one, apart from a stop to check out the long-staying bird that has been identified as an American Oystercatcher together with a Black Oystercatcher on the rocks along the western shore of the island, but we also did our best to check the birds on the breakwater, where we found moderate to large numbers of gulls, pelicans, and cormorants.  Also seen during this period were a couple of Mallards, a Spotted Sandpiper, a Royal Tern, three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons, a Great Blue Heron, two Snowy Egrets, and the usual small numbers of pigeons, crows, and Barn Swallows, along with some unseen Swinhoe’s White-Eyes and a hummingbird that were calling from trees on the island.  The Black-vented Shearwaters included on this list were noted just before we ended the list, but barely inside the outer buoy.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.12 kilometers, which was converted by the eBird system to a one-way distance of 3.97 kilometers for our trip through the harbor and just offshore (compensating for the loop we made in the channel to check out the oystercatchers).  On our departure from the harbor this morning, we had partly cloudy skies, with a 10-20% cover of high, thin clouds, humid and calm conditions, and a rather balmy temperature of 75° F on our arrival at the port (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle).  We further noted on the inshore waters just beyond the breakwater a swell of three feet from the southwest and a rippled surface.  Conditions during this period at the Capistrano Beach Nearshore buoy, located at 33° 26’ 43” N, 117° 40’ 49” W, about two kilometers northeast of where we ended this leg of the trip, represented a wave height of 1.2-1.4 meters [= 3.9-4.6 feet], with a dominant period from the south-southwest of 18 seconds and an average period ranging 10.1-11.7 seconds, and unusually warm water, given a temperature of 25.7° C [= 78.3° F], on the basis of data taken from the NOAA website for buoy data.  7:10-7:40 am. On our return to port this afternoon, we passed through the harbor mouth at about 4:00 pm, and then through the main harbor channel at moderate speed, along the way checking the birds on the outer breakwater, on and over the channel, and along the shore of the island.  This list began after we reached the shallow, inshore waters at a depth of about 30 meters approximately 1¾ kilometers essentially due south of the tip of the Dana Point breakwater (33° 26’ 39” N, 117° 43’ 06” W), and it ended when we disembarked after reaching the dock at 4:11 pm.  Given that we passed through the harbor relatively quickly without stopping, this list is best considered an incomplete survey of the birds that were likely present around the harbor during our visit.  We nevertheless saw good numbers of both Heermann’s and Western Gulls, but only one Elegant Tern, many cormorants and pelicans, along with a Black Oystercatcher, two Spotted Sandpipers, six Snowy Egrets and an adult Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, many pigeons, a Eurasian Collared-Dove, and an American Crow, along with five Mallards and an Osprey, the latter perched in a eucalyptus tree on the island.  Benson also recorded two each Red-necked Phalaropes and Black-vented Shearwaters just off the harbor.  The eBird app on Benson’s phone tracked our total distance at 4.4 kilometers, which was unchanged by the eBird system, indicating no backtracking along our one-way trip.  It was mostly clear, with a &lt;5% cover of high, thin clouds, a swell from the west to the southwest of 2-3 feet, and a rippled surface offshore, and a mild (5-10 knot) breeze from the southwest, and a temperature of 84° F on our return to port (on the basis of the thermometer in Benson’s vehicle). Rare bird for the region. Initially undocumented on checklist while awaiting photo review and confirmation. Now submitted with multiple clear images.--Field Marks Supporting YCNH over juvenile Black-crowned Night-Heron:- • Head and Bill: Thick, blunt bill with a slightly paler base and prominent reddish-orange eye, diagnostic for Yellow-crowned. Black-crowned juveniles typically show a slimmer, more tapered bill and duller eyes.- • Plumage: Coarse, bold vertical streaking on the neck and underparts, as well as finely barred coverts on the upper wings. The streaks on this bird are buffy and broad — not the narrower, more teardrop-shaped streaking seen on BCNH.- • Posture and Proportions: Bird held a more elongated neck, taller stance, and upright posture typical of Yellow-crowned. BCNH usually appears stockier and more hunched, with a shorter neck.- • Flight Structure: In-flight shots show broad, rounded wings with minimal contrast between inner and outer flight feathers, and longer, dangling legs. Yellow-crowned typically shows a more uniform wing coloration than BCNH

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS3076457311	2025-04-20 18:46:00.984349	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1					United States	US	California	US-CA	Sacramento	US-CA-067		32			North Natomas Regional Park	L10185202	H	38.6639521	-121.5164887	2025-04-20	10:55:00	obsr1010058		S227604194	Traveling	Traveling	P22			124	2.736		1	1		0	1	1			Continuing rarity re-found a few days ago by Kelli O'Neill, back for its third known season at the north Natomas heron and egret rookery. When I arrived the bird was resting, making very little movements on a horizontal branch near the top of the Eastmost willow on the West Island. Its eyes were closed and its long neck was tucked in. I could see the all black head interrupted by a white cheek patch that is widest and circular at the back of the cheek but narrows to a point at the front. Medium sized gray bill. The forehead of the bird is a rich daisy yellow color. The body of the bird is all smooth gray with black triangular streaks on the back. The legs are bright pink. I noticed a collection of twigs by its feet. --Detailed notes about its behavior: --About around 11 am, the bird awoke, lifted its long neck, and I could see its reddish orange eye. The six or seven long and thin white plume feathers on the back of its head raised to be almost completely vertical. The bird began to display, all of its feathers fluffed up, making the bird bigger. Its extraordinary long slender back plumes raised. The bird then opened its wings and bowed, the bottom of its neck lowering the farthest, its lower back lifting. Then the bird returned to its normal posture. It displayed to no noticeable bird a few times, then a Black Crowned Night Heron flew on its branch in front of it. The YCNH changed positions and displayed facing the BCNH (and also facing me). From the front the bird's display is gorgeous, its raised spidery back plumes create the illusion that the bird is wearing a giant Mohawk. The YCNH displayed once for the BCNH, and then the BCNH flew off. The YCNH began climbing down from its perch, and displayed for other BCNH perched lower in the willow. None of them indicated interest. The YCNH then flew down to the bottom of the island, and walked towards the trunk of a Sycamore. It then picked up a longish twig below the tree. It kept setting it down and picking it back up, before leaving it entirely. The heron began to walk back towards the base of the willow, but was spooked by a sitting Canada Goose that struck its elongated neck toward it with its bill open. The heron hopped backwards in response and began walking north of the willow, and disappeared down the back slope of the island. It re-appeared up the slope with another twig in its bill, and flew back to its spot in the willow. The bird then lowered the twig into the pile by its feet and shuffled it into the pile, shaking its head slightly, perhaps to help weave the stick into the makeshift nest. The bird also maneuvered different twigs around to perhaps make the new one fit better. After it was done, it displayed a few more times with its back to me, then resumed resting in place. I did not get pictures.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS626270629	2025-10-12 01:54:28.987215	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1				Unknown Sex, Adult (1)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Bernardino	US-CA-071		32			Prado Regional Park	L384807	H	33.9463861	-117.6506138	2018-05-28	10:30:00	obsr54638		S46202926	Traveling	Traveling	P22			210	1.000		4	0	G3240705	1	1	1			This was a boldly marked bird with the head pattern dominating the patterns.  The forehead and forecrown were rich, butter-yellow in color blending to a creamy-yellow to whitish as it tapered and extended back across the crown to the nape.  The longest plumes were white, but I thought some of the shorter plumes may have been dark.  Contrasting sharply with the paler forehead and crown, the lores, supraloral and superciliary regions, and the lower parts of the face were a dull black in color.  Complementing the cream-colored crown was a comma-shaped band of this same color that began narrowly right under the eye and then extended more broadly backward across the auriculars before ending in a rounded terminus at the rear edge of the auriculars.  Below the whitish stripe, the lower part of the face and the throat were again dull black, as was the side of the upper neck immediately behind the auriculars.  Demarcating the boldly marked head, the neck was an unmarked, medium-gray color down to the breast and back.  The underparts were this same medium-gray from the breast and sides down across the belly, flanks, and probably the undertail coverts, though my recollection of the latter is not as good.  I also noted a few dusky streaks on the belly that were relatively inconspicuous, yet bolder than I can recall seeing on this species in the past.--Returning to the upperparts, the coloration of the back and wings combined slate-gray to blackish centers with medium-gray fringes.  On the back and scapulars, the feathers were slate-gray to dull blackish with medium-gray edges that were well-defined and of roughly comparable width from the base to the tip of each tapered feather, which resulted in a series of V-shaped markings.  Further apparent were several long, conspicuously narrow, and filamentous plumes that extended almost to the wingtips and which again had slate-gray to blackish shaft-stripes that contrasted with medium-gray edges that had a frayed appearance.  The rather small lesser-coverts near the shoulder had slate-gray centers that contrasted with narrow but well-defined fringes that created a scaly pattern.  The coloration of the medina coverts was similar, but their larger size and more tapered shape resulted in two or three rows of V-shaped markings across the middle part of the wing.  The greater coverts, however, had slate-gray centers that contrasted with a light gray fringe along the outer web of each feather but a much weaker edge to the inner web to create a row of sharply defined stripes along the lower, middle part of the wing.  I am not sure I ever clearly saw the primary coverts, but there were some dull, blackish feathers along the leading edge of the wing that presumably represented the alula and associated feathers.  Also apparent was what appeared to be more whitish, marginal wing-coverts that appeared as a band of whitish extending along leaving edge of the slightly spread wing.  I thought the pattern on the tertials and maybe one or two of the innermost secondaries was like that on the greater coverts, given narrow fringes of light gray contrasting sharply with slate-gray to blackish centers, but my impression was that the fringes on these feathers extended the length of both the inner and outer webs and around the tip of each feather.  The remaining remiges, representing most of the secondaries and seemingly all of the primaries, were again dusky gray to sooty in color, but these feathers had only inconspicuously paler edges to the outer webs that appeared more brownish of buffy in color.  I noted both that the tail was dark and that it did not contrast strongly with the closed wings, but I saw no more detail than this.--The bill was entirely black from base to tip, the eyes were a deep reddish-orange in color and surrounded by a dark orbital-ring, and the legs were a dull yellowish color when seen from behind and on the toes, but from the front, the legs were a dusky grayish in color.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS798729199	2025-10-12 03:11:59.10046	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1					United States	US	California	US-CA	San Bernardino	US-CA-071		32			Prado Regional Park	L384807	H	33.9463861	-117.6506138	2019-08-20	09:10:00	obsr54638		S59144780	Traveling	Traveling	P22			30	0.100		3	0		1	1	1			Given that Dick had already located the continuing night-heron prior to our arrival, we had no problem seeing this bird as soon as we arrived in the vicinity of the boat docks.  We spent a few minutes looking at this bird and I took a few photos as it perched in to open on a dead branch immediately across the lake, but it moved out of sight after only a few minutes.  I relocated the heron a few minutes later as it perched in a more obscured location on or near the same branch but in the shade amid the vegetation of the willows, where it remained for the duration of our visit.  The views through my scope were good, but the distance was a bit much for good photos, especially when the bird was partially obscured.--This was a medium-sized heron with a blocky head, stocky body, seemingly short wings, relatively long and moderately stout legs, and a generally heavy bill that was a little longer than the head was wide and tapering from a deep base to a pointed tip along a subtly yet smoothly decurved culmen.  I further noted that the forehead was short and inconspicuous, and that the crown was gently rounded to somewhat flattened with a short plume extending back from the rear terminus of the crown, but given that this bird was in a relaxed position with the neck retracted, it was impossible to gain an appreciation of the length or mass or the neck, and some of the details of the head shape.  I also failed to notice in detail the primary projection and placement of the wingtips relative to the tail when this bird was facing away from me, yet my impression was that the wings were short and rounded, with minimal primary projection and wingtips that were about as long as the tail--This was a relatively boldly marked bird that was generally typical of an adult Yellow-crowned Night-Heron in its patterns and coloration.  I noted, for example, that the head was almost entirely a dull black in color, including the supraloral and superciliary regions, the lower part of the face, and the entire throat.  Contrasting sharply with the mostly black head was a subtly curved, creamy-white crescent that extended back from a point just below the eye across the auriculars, curving upward and expanding slightly as it crossed the lower part of the auriculars to their rear terminus.  Somewhat atypical for an adult of this species, the forehead and crown were mostly blackish centrally, yet with narrow lines of cream to pale yellowish extending along either side of the forehead and crown and tapering inward to frame the dark center of the crown.  I also thought the plume that extended backward from the rear part of the crown was dark as opposed to white.  The black-and-whitish head was sharply demarcated by a medium-gray neck that appeared to lack markings altogether.  The underparts were similarly colored, but I noted a few relatively fine, dark streaks on the belly that I do not usually associate with an adult of this species.--Returning to the upperparts, what I could see of the back, scapulars, and wing coverts appeared to have a strong pattern that combined blackish centers to feathers that had narrow yet well-defined edges of light gray that tapered inward distally as a result of what appeared to be generally wedge-shaped feathers.  I did not see the remiges quite as well as the coverts, but what I did see appeared to combine dark gray centers with edges that were weaker than those of the coverts either because they were narrower or not as pale a gray.--The bill was mostly black, but with a paler and possibly yellowish stripe that extended maybe halfway out the center of the lower mandible.  The irides were either reddish or orangey-red and thus contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs and toes appeared to be a relatively dark gray to grayish-horn in color, though there may have been some yellowish tones to the “knee” joints.

Overcast to clearing, 62°/72°F. o.o: Priscilla Summers	The sub-adult or first summer YELLOW-CROWNED NIGHT-HERON has been around here since about 20 June. We got very good looks at it and I took several photos. The most notable field marks separating it from Black-crowned Night-Heron were the very stout, thick shorter bill, longer legs and neck, and the beginnings of an adult face pattern. The bird was overall somewhat mottled gray with a bright orange eye. There was a distinctive cream colored crown stripe and a cream colored stripe under the eye starting at the base of the bill and extending beyond the eye. The wing coverts were gray with black centers. The legs were black or dark on the front and yellowish on the back. The breast had several streaks of the same cream color.

The two --adult Yellow-crowned Night-Herons were in their usual spot in the middle of --the apartment parking lot east of the visitors center.----Along Seacoast Drive a Peregrine Falcon attacked a Clapper Rail, forcing it --into the water. It would dive under the water everytime the falcon swooped down. --At one point it appears the falcon "punched" the rail causing it to flip and --float with its legs in the air. At first glance it appeared to be a pure male "Yellow-shafted" --Flicker (yellow undersides to flight feathers, brown face with gray cap) but --closer inspection revealed the malar stripes to be maroon, not black, and --the red nape patch was reduced forming more of a thin "V" than a crescent. --Photos posted at the end of the miscellaneous folder:----http://ph.groups.yahoo.com/group/SDBIRDS/photos/browse/cfb0	the two adults in apt parking lot

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS56452681	2021-04-01 03:09:04.302999	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1					United States	US	California	US-CA	San Diego	US-CA-073	US-CA_256	32	USFWS_74		Tijuana Slough NWR	L265929	P	32.5710707	-117.1290303	2008-08-15	09:05:00	obsr98373		S4074379	Traveling	Traveling	P22			80	1.561		1	1		0	1	1		I got a good view of the yellow-crowned night heron''s face and back when it was in flight.  On the face, I clearly saw a line of black under the line of white, which was under a line of black.  The back was all the same shade of gray, unlike the two-color pattern on black-crowned.  I talked to someone at the visitor center who verified that indeed there have been a pair of yellow-crowned night-herons nesting in a local apartment building (where I saw the bird flying to), for the third consecutive year. URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS155580711	2025-03-29 16:36:18.055862	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				3	ON	C4	ON	Unknown Sex, Adult (3)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Diego	US-CA-073		32			Imperial Beach Sports Park	L586477	H	32.5756124	-117.1235004	2012-05-20	06:25:00	obsr54638		S10926095	Traveling	Traveling	P22			10	0.200		2	1		0	1	1			Given that Guy knew precisely where to look, we managed to see three of the adult birds in association with two different nests, one in a large pine and another in a broad-leaf ornamental over the parking lot.  I was able to note among these birds the large size, stocky body, blocky head with a somewhat flat-crowned appearance, and a rather massive bill that tapered from a heavy base to a pointed tip.  I think I saw all three birds well enough to see the clean-gray body and, on at least one of these birds, I saw clearly the paler gray fringes on the coverts and remiges that created both a scaly pattern to the upper part of the wings and a striped pattern to the lower part.  On at least two of these birds I was able to make out the bold pattern on the head that combined a yellowish forehead and crown, the mostly black sides of the head, and a whitish stripe across the face that began narrowly below the eye before broadening as it extended across the auriculars.  I used my 10 × 42 binoculars to study these birds, which we saw under the muted light that resulted from the overcast skies.  Given that I have seen these birds repeatedly over the course of the last several years, I did not study them all that carefully and I then waited several weeks to write a description, so my recollection of these birds is a bit fuzzier, and thus my description somewhat more superficial, than usual.  I can say confidently, however, that we saw all three birds well enough to identify them unequivocally as adult Yellow-crowned Night-Herons.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS188702686	2025-10-12 12:37:32.483518	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				2	ON	C4	ON	Unknown Sex, Adult (2)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Diego	US-CA-073		32			Imperial Beach Sports Park	L586477	H	32.5756124	-117.1235004	2013-04-02	07:15:00	obsr54638		S13614770	Traveling	Traveling	P22			20	0.200		2	1	G583648	0	1	1			It took some effort, but Dick eventually spotted one of the nesting pairs of Yellow-crowned Night-Herons in a densely vegetated pine along the western fence line of the park.  I studied these birds only briefly before we continued on our way, and we never did locate the second nesting pair.  One bird was sitting on a nest and the other was perched less than a meter away on a nearby branch.  We never heard these birds, which remained essentially motionless during our visit and, in general, with one of the birds facing away from us.  Both birds were plump herons of medium size with short wings and tails.  The bird on the nest had the typical, massive bill of this species that tapered from a heavy base to a bluntly pointed tip along a slightly decurved culmen, but I was unable to see this bird's legs.  The second bird was facing away, so it was difficult to see much of the bill, though what I did see was similar to that of the bird on the nest.  This bird also had medium-length legs that were relatively stout.--Both birds were a medium-gray color overall, but they had a boldly striped appearance that resulted from well-defined fringes of whitish to pale yellow on the wing coverts and remiges.  I think I saw the underparts only on the bird on the nest and what I saw appeared to be gray an unmarked.  I noted on the bird on the nest that the forehead and crown were creamy-yellow with the forehead somewhat more deeply colored, and that there was a complementary band of pale yellow to creamy-whitish that extended across the lower part of the face, but the head was otherwise blackish.  On the perched bird, I noted only an indication of the yellow forehead, pale facial stripe, and generally black head, but my views of this bird's head were not very good.  The bird seen best appeared to have an entirely black bill and, as I recall, reddish eyes, but I cannot now recall seeing the soft-part colored in any more detail.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS231935284	2025-03-29 16:36:18.055862	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				3				Unknown Sex, Adult (3)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Diego	US-CA-073		32			Imperial Beach Sports Park	L586477	H	32.5756124	-117.1235004	2014-01-23	14:45:00	obsr54638		S16739747	Area	Area	P23			25		4.0000	2	1	G798884	0	1	1			I spotted first one and then two more adult birds perched in the pines over the parking lot in the apartment complex immediately west of the park.  We were then invited by one of the residents to observe these birds from the complex, and once here, we discovered that one of the birds was standing in the open in good light.  Having seen these birds so many times over the last few years, I did not study them all that carefully, yet I saw each of the three more than well enough to make a definitive identification.  These were medium-sized herons with large and somewhat blocky heads, massive bills, retracted necks, and plump bodies with an upright posture, short wings, and even shorter tails.  I must admit that my views were restricted to the head, neck, and underparts on two of these birds, but the one we photographed was standing fully in the open.  It was only on this bird that I saw the moderately long, stout legs.--All three birds had blackish heads with the forehead and crown pale, and a whitish stripe that extended from just below the eye back across the auriculars.  I also noted on the bird we saw best a long, filamentous plume extending back and down from the crown.  The neck and underparts were medium-gray and unmarked, but the back and wings were a somewhat darker shade of gray with well-defined edges of light gray that created a boldly striped pattern to at least the wing coverts and remiges.  I cannot now recall if I ever saw a primary projection, and I am pretty sure I never clearly saw the tail.  The bill was entirely black and the legs were yellowish, but I cannot now recall the color of the eyes.  I noted a similar pattern on the head of the other two birds, and that both had unmarked, gray underparts, but I cannot recall seeing the upperparts well on these birds as they roosted in locations that were harder to see clearly.----<iframe src="https://www.flickr.com/photos/cmarantz/12315952824/player/0b60b270c5" height="533" width="800" frameborder="0"></iframe>
