URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS303350160	2025-03-29 16:36:18.055862	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				3				Unknown Sex, Adult (1); Unknown Sex, Immature (2)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Diego	US-CA-073		32			Imperial Beach Sports Park	L586477	H	32.5756124	-117.1235004	2015-03-13	10:55:00	obsr54638		S22368066	Area	Area	P23			10		1.0000	3	0	G1181136	0	1	1			Shortly after we began our search for the resident night-herons Paul located three birds roosting in a broadleaf tree at the edge of the parking lot near the restrooms.  As I recall, this is one of the trees in which these birds have nested in past seasons.  The adult was standing near a nest, but I am not sure these birds have begun preparing their nest for the up[conign season.  The two young birds were perched singly not too far away, but also in the upper branches of the trees amid the moderately dense vegetation.  The angle was less than ideal for observing these birds from below, yet we were able to see more than enough to identify them and I even took a few photos.--All three birds were stocky herons with rather massive bills, blocky heads with what appeared a steep forehead and a somewhat flattened crown, at least on the adult, which I saw best.  All three birds had the neck retracted, and all three had a plump body, a full-chested appearance, and an upright posture.  The wings and tail both appeared to be relatively short, btu the legs were long and stout.--The adult bird had a blackish head with a butter-yellow forehead, but I could not clearly see the crown and I cannot now recall even seeing the pale stripe on the face.  The underparts were a medium-gray color and apparently unmarked.  I saw only the leading edge and some of the side of the wings, yet I was able to note that the coverts and remiges were dark gray with lighter gray fringes that extended down the edges and across the tips of the greater coverts to create a pattern or elongate rectangles.  The remiges were similarly marked, but because I was unable to see the tips of these feathers I thought the pattern was one of well-defined stripes along the leading edge of the wing.  The bil appeared to be entirely dull black and the legs were pale.  I saw this bird’s eyes, but I cannot now recall their coloration.--The young birds were quite a dark shade of gray above and dull whitish below with bold streaks of about the same shade of dark gray as the upperparts.  I noted on at least one of these birds a pattern on the wing coverts and remiges that was much like that of the adult, but with the centers of the feathers even darker and the fringes maybe not so purely light gray.  The head was generally quite dark but also with a somewhat streaked appearance.  As I recall, both of these birds had entirely black bills, but I cannot recall noting the color of the eyes or legs in the field.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS466260456	2025-03-29 16:36:18.055862	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				7	ON	C4	ON	Unknown Sex, Immature (1); Unknown Sex, Adult (6)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Diego	US-CA-073		32			Imperial Beach Sports Park	L586477	H	32.5756124	-117.1235004	2017-02-12	10:55:00	obsr227469		S34410262	Area	Area	P23			15		0.5000	4	1	G2207404	1	1	0			Guy located the resident night-herons within minutes of our arrival at the park today.  We then spent several minutes studying these birds and taking a few photos before continuing on our way.  All of the Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that we saw today were in a single, broadleaf tree located over the parking lot in the northwestern part of the park.  We saw at least two adults standing atop nests and one or two additional nests located not far from where other birds were perched in the tree.  In all, we saw six adult birds and one first-winter individual.  I took photos of at least one of these birds, but I studied the others at least relatively carefully.  Below is a composite description of what I noted on the various adults during this encounter.--These were medium-sized herons with stocky bodies, large heads, and massive bills that tapered from a base that was both wide and deep to a blunt tip.  Given that we were looking up at these birds, it was difficult to discern their precise shape, but my impression was that the crown was relatively flattened and I noted on at least one or two of these birds one or two filamentous plumes extending back from the nape.  These birds also appeared to have relatively short wings that extended roughly to the tip of the tail, and medium-length legs that were at least moderately stout.--The adults were generally a medium-gray color overall and with little or no markings on the underparts.  Rather striking was a head pattern that combined a butter-yellow forehead with a creamy to whitish crown and a complementary band of white across the lower part of the face.  Contrasting with the pale regions of the face was the black of the lower and rear parts of the head and the superciliary region.  I noted on at least one bird one or two filamentous, white plumes extended back from the nape.  The wing coverts and remiges were dark gray with well-defined edges of light gray to whitish that produced a boldly striped pattern to the wings overall.  Given that I was looking up at these birds, I am not sure how well I ever saw their backs, but even if I did, I cannot now recall much about them.  I noted that the bill of each bird on which I saw it clearly was mostly black, but I am not sure the degree to which the base of the lower mandible may have been paler.  I also have only a vague recollection that the eyes were dark and that the legs were greenish.--The immature bird was a medium to dark gray in color, but quite dingy overall, and with a somewhat mottled appearance below.  This bird also had whitish to pale gray fringes to the wing coverts and remiges that resulted in a somewhat striped pattern, yet one that was more subtle than that on the adults as a result of the edges appearing worn and relatively thin.  This bird also had at least one white plume extending back from the nape, and its overall size and structure were similar to those of the adults.  I noted on this bird that the eyes were an odd shade of orange.  The bill was at least mostly black, but again, I am not sure to what degree the lower mandible may have been paler.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS465535526	2025-03-29 16:36:18.055862	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				7	ON	C4	ON	Unknown Sex, Immature (1); Unknown Sex, Adult (6)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Diego	US-CA-073		32			Imperial Beach Sports Park	L586477	H	32.5756124	-117.1235004	2017-02-12	10:55:00	obsr54638		S34350633	Area	Area	P23			15		0.5000	4	1	G2207404	1	1	0			Guy located the resident night-herons within minutes of our arrival at the park today.  We then spent several minutes studying these birds and taking a few photos before continuing on our way.  All of the Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that we saw today were in a single, broadleaf tree located over the parking lot in the northwestern part of the park.  We saw at least two adults standing atop nests and one or two additional nests located not far from where other birds were perched in the tree.  In all, we saw six adult birds and one first-winter individual.  I took photos of at least one of these birds, but I studied the others at least relatively carefully.  Below is a composite description of what I noted on the various adults during this encounter.--These were medium-sized herons with stocky bodies, large heads, and massive bills that tapered from a base that was both wide and deep to a blunt tip.  Given that we were looking up at these birds, it was difficult to discern their precise shape, but my impression was that the crown was relatively flattened and I noted on at least one or two of these birds one or two filamentous plumes extending back from the nape.  These birds also appeared to have relatively short wings that extended roughly to the tip of the tail, and medium-length legs that were at least moderately stout.--The adults were generally a medium-gray color overall and with little or no markings on the underparts.  Rather striking was a head pattern that combined a butter-yellow forehead with a creamy to whitish crown and a complementary band of white across the lower part of the face.  Contrasting with the pale regions of the face was the black of the lower and rear parts of the head and the superciliary region.  I noted on at least one bird one or two filamentous, white plumes extended back from the nape.  The wing coverts and remiges were dark gray with well-defined edges of light gray to whitish that produced a boldly striped pattern to the wings overall.  Given that I was looking up at these birds, I am not sure how well I ever saw their backs, but even if I did, I cannot now recall much about them.  I noted that the bill of each bird on which I saw it clearly was mostly black, but I am not sure the degree to which the base of the lower mandible may have been paler.  I also have only a vague recollection that the eyes were dark and that the legs were greenish.--The immature bird was a medium to dark gray in color, but quite dingy overall, and with a somewhat mottled appearance below.  This bird also had whitish to pale gray fringes to the wing coverts and remiges that resulted in a somewhat striped pattern, yet one that was more subtle than that on the adults as a result of the edges appearing worn and relatively thin.  This bird also had at least one white plume extending back from the nape, and its overall size and structure were similar to those of the adults.  I noted on this bird that the eyes were an odd shade of orange.  The bill was at least mostly black, but again, I am not sure to what degree the lower mandible may have been paler.

The latest checklist removes the hyphen from "Night-Heron." Typically hyphenated names indicate monophyletic groups while removing the hyphen indicates otherwise. In this case there are some more distantly related herons also called Night Herons, thus the hyphen was removed from all of them. The characteristic large swollen bill is specialized for eating crabs. They have expanded their range with multiple pairs breeding in coastal Southern California as far north as Ventura County. Their first successful California nesting was in 2006 at San Diego. This is the subspecies "N. v. bancrofti" characterized by paler coloration, narrower dorsal streaks and having a thicker bill than the nominate East Coast race.

Obvious Flycatcher due to perched behavior, flight behavior, and spectrograph of call. Included coords in the species notes. --Overcast and light rain. Low 70s.	Flew in at Preserve area around dusk to hunt.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS534092533	2017-09-21 09:10:23	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1				Unknown Sex, Juvenile (1)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Luis Obispo	US-CA-079	US-CA_145				Morro Bay SP--Marina/Boardwalk Trail	L1316658	H	35.3445235	-120.8418006	2017-09-18	19:11:00	obsr53921		S39265201	Incidental	Incidental	P20						2	0		0	1	1		Curtis Marantz and I quickly walked the marina near dusk looking for the Yellow-crowned Night-Herons reported here. We saw one, the bird with typical patterning for juvenile Yellow-crown. Light fog; strong breeze 10-15 mph W; tide mid to low and rising; quick check of the marina.	Perched on a boat at the western end of the marina where several Black-crowned Night-Herons also were perched. Even in the dim light, this bird was a cold gray color overall with crisp streaking in the face and on the underparts. The crown was likewise streaked with thin pale lines but on a blacker background. The streaks on the underparts were sharply blackish against a whitish background. I noted that the greater wing coverts were tipped with small dots of white and the outer margin of these coverts was thinly but distinctly margined with pale cream or white, this forming a lattice-like pattern across the wing. The remaining wing coverts and scapulars were also tipped with small white dots. I did note that the pattern in the very midline back was more obscure and that the actual back feathers were plainer gray, with perhaps only the tiniest of white dots. This is typical of Yellow-crowned Night-Heron. (This bird, however, was not the one of two here that has freshly molted back feathers that are plain.)----The bird appeared smaller and particularly of slighter, rangier build than a juvenile Black-crowned nearby. The bill was blunt and thick and all black (or nearly all black so that in this light I could not see any obvious pale coloration at the base of the mandible). The rear end of the bird appeared to sit higher on the legs versus Black-crowned, which when squat has its rear (tip of tail) further down the legs. This made the Yellow-crowned look taller, even though I could not assess the actual leg length difference. The bill of Black-crowned was clearly longer, tapered to a sharp tip, and slightly decurved. The Black-crowned also showed obvious pale on most of the mandible.----Nothing about the features of this bird suggested past hybridization with Black-crowned. One Yellow-crowned Night-Heron was first reported here 13 September by Linda Dalton (fide Tom Edell). Two were then seen on the 14th. These constitute the first record of this species for San Luis Obispo County and one of only three records north of Santa Barbara County in California (San Rafael, Marin Co. from mid July 1968 continuing/returning through mid Oct 1973; 12 Sep-17 Oct 1981 at Año Nuevo State Reserve, San Mateo Co.; two reports not accepted from northern CA include birds at Tomales Bay, Marin Co., and at Bodega Bay, Sonoma Co.; there is also a report not accepted from Furnace Creek, Inyo Co., per Hamilton et al. 2007).

With Kathy Molina. Parking area, marina, boardwalk trail out to the point; I did not use a scope, so lots of unidentified distant shorebirds, etc. in bay to south. Mostly clear, tide medium-low; 60 deg F.	Continuing juveniles, easily studied as they perched on boats in the easternmost part of the marina. Darkish coloration, distinct small triangles (rather than larger teardrop spots) on slaty coverts, long yellowish legs and thick mostly black bills made identification straightforward. One of the birds had a bit more yellowish on the bill base than the other and it might have been a bit paler dorsally. The attached photos show both birds.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS853647943	2025-07-06 19:10:19.181585	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1				Unknown Sex, Immature (1)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Luis Obispo	US-CA-079					Morro Bay harbor mouth	L291269	H	35.3640786	-120.8658353	2020-01-18	15:10:00	obsr54638		S63579749	Traveling	Traveling	P22			40	2.278		40	0	G4890762	0	1	1			While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS854452486	2025-07-06 18:27:50.891005	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1				Unknown Sex, Immature (1)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Luis Obispo	US-CA-079					Morro Bay harbor mouth	L291269	H	35.3640786	-120.8658353	2020-01-18	15:10:00	obsr324500		S63646315	Traveling	Traveling	P22			40	2.278		40	0	G4890762	0	1	1		Tom Edell, Curtis Marantz, Wes Fritz, and Will Knowlton led the full-day pelagic trip for the Morro Bay Winter Bird Festival aboard the M/V Endeavor out of the Morro Bay Landing with Brad Leage as captain.  The present list is for our return trip through the harbor and inshore waters out to the outermost buoy at the mouth of the harbor.  We cruised through the harbor relatively quickly, so even though we did our best to see what was present, this is best considered an incomplete survey of the many birds that were present on a relatively low tide with exposed mudflats along the sandspit.  We arrived at the dock at 3:25 pm, but then spent an extended period of time at the dock going over the lists for the day.  We saw both Long-tailed Ducks, but we did not stop to study either of them carefully.  The obvious highlight, but seen by only the leaders at the dock after participants had left, was an immature Yellow-crowned Night-Heron that was spotted by Fritz at the dock.  Also onboard were local birders Maggie Smith, Herb Elliott, and Pat and Ann Vaughan, Jeff Miller, Norman Pillsbury, but most participants were from out of town.  Edell's eBird Android phone app calculated the one-way distance through the harbor at 1.42 miles.  There was a roughly 95% cover of high clouds, a moderate (10-15 knot), breeze from the northeast, from which we were largely sheltered when at the dock, and a temperature of 57° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Edell’s vehicle).  3:10-4:00 pm.----Sea Otter - 18 (this is an estimate).	While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS854109567	2025-07-06 18:42:39.473762	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1				Unknown Sex, Immature (1)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Luis Obispo	US-CA-079					Morro Bay harbor mouth	L291269	H	35.3640786	-120.8658353	2020-01-18	15:10:00	obsr660022		S63616731	Traveling	Traveling	P22			40	2.278		40	0	G4890762	0	1	1			While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS854108333	2025-07-06 18:42:40.003104	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1				Unknown Sex, Immature (1)	United States	US	California	US-CA	San Luis Obispo	US-CA-079					Morro Bay harbor mouth	L291269	H	35.3640786	-120.8658353	2020-01-18	15:10:00	obsr659479		S63616627	Traveling	Traveling	P22			40	2.278		40	0	G4890762	0	1	1		Tom Edell, Curtis Marantz, Wes Fritz, and Will Knowlton led the full-day pelagic trip for the Morro Bay Winter Bird Festival aboard the M/V Endeavor out of the Morro Bay Landing with Brad Leage as captain.  The present list is for our return trip through the harbor and inshore waters out to the outermost buoy at the mouth of the harbor.  We cruised through the harbor relatively quickly, so even though we did our best to see what was present, this is best considered an incomplete survey of the many birds that were present on a relatively low tide with exposed mudflats along the sandspit.  We arrived at the dock at 3:25 pm, but then spent an extended period of time at the dock going over the lists for the day.  We saw both Long-tailed Ducks, but we did not stop to study either of them carefully.  The obvious highlight, but seen by only the leaders at the dock after participants had left, was an immature Yellow-crowned Night-Heron that was spotted by Fritz at the dock.  Also onboard were local birders Maggie Smith, Herb Elliott, and Pat and Ann Vaughan, Jeff Miller, Norman Pillsbury, but most participants were from out of town.  Edell's eBird Android phone app calculated the one-way distance through the harbor at 1.42 miles.  There was a roughly 95% cover of high clouds, a moderate (10-15 knot), breeze from the northeast, from which we were largely sheltered when at the dock, and a temperature of 57° F (on the basis of the thermometer in Edell’s vehicle).  3:10-4:00 pm.----Sea Otter - 18 (this is an estimate).	While going through the lists for the day, Fritz spotted this bird standing on the dock below the landing at which we had just arrived and mere meters from where we departed the boat a few minutes earlier.  I then walked down onto the dock and took several photos before this bird flew to one of the braces for the building above, where it remained for us to take some more photos.  I never heard this bird vocalize and it was rather sedate while under observation apart from it sone short flight.  Not only was this bird a year older than the other three Yellow-crowned Night-Herons that were at the state park, but after seeing this bird we drove over to the state park marina and saw all three first-winter birds that have been there.--This was a stocky, medium-sized heron with a rather massive bill, a blocky head, a medium-length neck that was more massive than those of most herons yet slimmer than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron, short and seemingly rounded wings, a short tail, and medium-length legs that had more mass than those of an egret.  I thought the bill was quite deep and that it was about as long as the head was wide, with a culmen that curved subtly yet smoothly downward to the pointed tip of the bill.  The forehead was steep but short and the crown was gently rounded back to the more strongly rounded junction of the crown with the nape.  When extended, this bird’s neck was both long and slim for a night-heron even though it was both shorter and stouter than that of a egret.  The body was plump, full-chested, and with a posture that was more upright than diagonal when the bird was alert.  I noted minimal primary projection on short, rounded wings that appeared to fall right at the tip of the short tail, which was obscured by the closed wings.--This bird’s plumage patterns were clearly those of a subadult bird in that they combined a faint suggestion of the pattern of an adult on the head with the generally grayish or brownish body and wings of a young bird.  The head was generally a slate-gray in color, but with the forehead and crown brownish centrally yet with a paler and somewhat yellowish frame that extended through the supraloral region and along either side of the crown.  I also noted at least some suggestion of a pale gray stripe extending narrowly below the eye before expanding on the auriculars in a faint suggestion of the adult cheek-stripe.  The chin and maybe also the upper throat were pale yellow and thus contrasting conspicuously with the more blackish face.  I did not see the neck all that well, but it did not appear to contrast obviously with the body.  The back and scapulars was a medium to dark gray and each of the larger scapular feathers at least had a relatively broad band of slate gray running down the center that was bordered on either side by lighter gray to create a striped appearance to the generally dark and grayish upperparts.  The wings contrasted as lighter and slightly browner than the back, and at least most of the covert feathers had a small, pale spot where the shaft met the tip.  The larger greater coverts, and maybe also some of the lesser coverts also had a paler stripe along the leading edge that gave the lower part of the closed wing a striped appearance that was even more conspicuously given the narrow but well-defined fringes on the tertials.  I did not see the underparts as well as I did the upperparts and wings, but what I did see appeared to be quite dusky and seemingly not as conspicuously striped as were the first-winter birds seen shortly later.--The bill was a dull, blackish in color, and the irides were orangey and contrasting sharply with the black pupils.  The legs appeared to be blackish when seen from the front, but greenish or yellowish-green when seen from behind; however, I cannot now remember the color of the toes.

I saw it from Hwy 1 looking downstream into the creek.--Almost all dark face with perhaps a hint of a lighter cheek, unlike the distinctly two-toned, more pale-faced appearance of immature Black-crowned night herons. Bill large, dagger like, all dark and symmetric; lacking any yellowish tones to lower mandible. Probably have identifiable photos of the obscured bird.

During rising tide after a low tide about 2 hours earlier.	When I first arrived I saw 2 Yellow-crowned Night-heron juveniles perched on the fishing boat Rose Lynn, which was docked near the large parking lot. As I started to walk, one of them, then the other flew down from the boat to dock, then across the small amount of water to the rocky shore of boulders just down from the parking lot and below the sidewalk where I was. As I concentrated on one, I lost track of the other. The one I watched did some patient standing, then some side-to-side swaying of head, neck and sometimes body as it seemed to home in on its prey. I tried to get some video (links below) and witnessed the night-heron gradually stretch its neck forward and dart its bill at prey at the edges of these large rocks several times. It caught something quite small that I could not identify; missed on another attempt; caught, but then immediately lost a crab with large pinchers; then finally was successful at catching another crab. The heron briefly tried to orient the crab such that it could get it down its bill without removing any appendages and, while still holding the crab in its bill, flew to the nearest part of the dock where it continued trying to align the crab in its bill. After most of a minute it successfully swallowed the crab. Videos: https://www.flickr.com/photos/marlinharms/54811476588/--https://www.flickr.com/photos/marlinharms/54810327476/

Not very thorough coverage as I got distracted by the night heron. High numbers of raptors, as reported elsewhere in the bay today	Juvenile on the pond. Second record for this pond. I was scanning the pond and came across a night heron, and was shocked to see that it very gray in color. I ran back to my car to get my scope, and then was able to confirm it was a Yellow-crowned. Compared to Black-crowned, the overall color was very different, being a silvery-gray compared to the brown of a Black-crowned. The bill was very thick and entirely dark. The chin was white. The head was dark and covered in small white spots. The wings were also covered in small white spots. Unfortunately there was no service here, so i drove to pescadero to let people know. Sadly, the bird was no longer present when I got back to the pond about 35 minutes later. However, I think the bird is still very likely in the area, and is likely foraging in the pond during the early morning and late afternoon.

From main parking to  freshwater pond.	Previously reported. Present for more than a week, but few reports. Today, the bird was under observation by Chris and Malia when I arrived. It was at the extreme north end of the pond, up to 200 yards distant, standing or perching above water level, partially obscured by a few reeds. The overall color of the upperparts was dark grey-brown. There were some small white spots at the tips of the wing coverts and perhaps elswhere. I saw the bird the first day, but did not write up my observations due to an illness that struck me the next day. I returned to see the bird on 13 February, when I found it in the same area where I had seen it previously, in willows visible from a foot bridge leading across the creek to the Bacara Resort. The bird remained on the same branch, stationary, the entire time I was present. I watched it for 10 or 15 minutes, recorded my observations on my iPhone, and transcribed this description from those observations a month later. ----Description: A small, pale buffy area on the chin, but otherwise very gray below, wrapping around the auriculars, which were black surrounding a whitish area in the center. The crown was gray from the top of the bill backward to about mid-crown and appeared black from the center backward. My notes mentioned adult-like white plumes, but don¿t say anything about length of placement of the plumes. A brownish area could be seen adjacent to the bend in the wing. The wing coverts were gray and brown, with buffy edging to all of the these feathers, which also had dark feather shafts. The flight feathers weren¿t clearly visible; it did appear that they were dark, but it wasn¿t evident whether or not they had pale edges. I couldn¿t see the mantle and tail well.----The bill was mostly blackish or dark gray, but with a yellow area on the mandible concentrated at the base. It was longer than that of Black-crowned Night-Heron, and the culmen was more curved, giving the bill a slightly droopy look. The legs were also long compared to those of Black-crowned Night-Herons. The bird kept its eyes closed most of the time I watched it. The eyelid was gray, and the eye was dark orangish red.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS463703374	2021-03-18 23:47:51.951666	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1					United States	US	California	US-CA	Santa Barbara	US-CA-083		32			Bacara Resort And Spa	L3041789	H	34.4331068	-119.9162972	2010-03-12	13:05:00	obsr57292		S6123886	Stationary	Stationary	P21			20			1	1		1	1	1			Accepted by CBRC. Description: A mid-sized heron, approximately the same size as the nearby 5 or so Black-crowned Night-Herons. The body size was possibly a little bit slimmer than that species though. The bill was mostly black with a small amount of green near the base, and slightly shorter and stouter than that of a Black-crowned Night-Heron. The body plumage was almost entirely even slate-gray, with a slight wash of brown to some portions. The wing coverts and mantle feathers were all lanceolate in shape, each with a thin gray-brown border and a dark gray center. The tail was short and looked to be dark, but I did not take much note of it. The neck was short and the head was held close to the body, thus further accentuating the shortness of the neck. The throat and malar area were black, extending back to the lower nape to connect with very broad black supercilium. This area of black surrounded a broad whitish line that extended back from the eye through the auricular. The crown stripe was grayish-white, contrasting relatively little with the broad black supercilium. There were two short thin white plumes extending from the rear of the crown, and a small spot of white barely visible on the chin. The legs were lime green, and the eye was dark red.

URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS421102797	2018-08-03 08:27:27	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1					United States	US	California	US-CA	Santa Barbara	US-CA-083		32			Carpinteria Salt Marsh Nature Park	L3051348	H	34.3961231	-119.5283666	2016-07-22	19:45:00	obsr54638		S30866000	Traveling	Traveling	P22			25	0.400		1	1		1	1	1			I spotted this bird shortly after I began scanning the channel above the footbridge over Franklin Creek, where it remained for most of my visit before flying south down the channel at dusk.  I spent most of my time taking photos of this bird as it walked slowly and quietly in the shallow water.--This was a stocky heron of medium size with a bill that was heavy at the base and tapering little to a blunt tip,  I further noted that the bill was almost as long as the head was wide.  The forehead was steep for a short distance before curving sharply where it met the gently rounded crown to give the head a blocky appearance.  The neck was retracted, so it appeared short and inconspicuous, and the body was plump and with an upright posture.  The wings were short and rounded, reaching right about to the tip of the short tail, and with a primary projection that was almost imperceptible.  The legs appeared to be both stout and relatively short for a heron.  My views of the bird when it flew overhead were brief and insufficient to note any real detail.--This bird’s plumage was much like that of an adult, but close inspection revealed that it was not quite there.  The forehead and crown were a sooty-brown color, but with a creamy-white border that began in the supraloral region near the base of the bill and extended up over the eye and along the sides of the crown to the nape, from which there appeared to be a narrow plume that extended a short way over the nape.  Contrasting with the pale borders to the crown, the face was generally a dull black color, but also with a dull white stripe that extended narrowly back form the bill near the gape under the eye before expanding into an oval across the center of the auriculars that was bordered above below, and behind by the black of the sides of the head.  I also noted that the black extended from the nape a short way down the back of the neck.  Apart form this stripe, the back and sides of the neck were medium gray and unmarked.  when seen from the front, the neck and underparts were also medium-gray, but with both a dingy appearance that was unlike the pure gray of an adult and a jagged, dark stripe that extended down the foreneck to the breast.  The back, scapulars, and wing coverts were boldly marked with each feather having a slate-gray center that contrasted with light gray edges that were well-defined as they extended down both the inner and outer edges to create a series of “V-shaped” markings given the tapered shape of these feathers.  Also apparent was a combination of new feathers that were more purely gray and older feathers that were faded, paler, and more brownish, but each with a similar pattern.  The tertials had slate-gray centers that contrasted with light gray edges, but the secondaries below appeared to be lighter and more brownish.  I never clearly saw the tail.--The bill was entirely black, the irides were a deep orange, and the legs were a deep, mustard-yellow in color.

My intent was to find hummingbirds nesting, hence my off trail route. I found none. Yellow-crowned Night-Heron may not have been detected at Campus Lagoon previously. Weather: in the low 70s F, no wind, clear. <a href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/91666839@N00/39935258333/in/dateposted/" title="Campus Lagoon 27 Jan 2019"><img src="https://farm8.staticflickr.com/7852/39935258333_50f680acf5_m.jpg" alt="Campus Lagoon 27 Jan 2019" /></a> Click on image to enlarge it.	Compared to other night-herons present in the willow patch on the north side of the lagoon, this bird was over all grayish in tone, although breast was not well seen.  I viewed it by spotting scope from the south side of the lagoon looking north. The bird was at 34.40877 -119.84605. Bill was slightly stubbier than other herons present and grayish-black with minimal pale color at the base of the mandible. Those breast streaks that are visible seem thin and not blurry.  Spots on the wings seem small and round, not tear-drop shaped. The greater wing coverts show a white margin on their outer edge. Perhaps this is the first sighting for Campus Lagoon.  The other night-herons present should be checked more carefully than I was able to do today.

Rose and I started in the Goleta Beach Park parking lot east of Sandspit Rd. and observed the southern side of the Goleta water channel. We drove to the parking lot west of Sandspit and took the paved path at the north side of the lot, across the wooden Rock Pigeon bridge and back. We walked on the bike path east and crossed Sandspit bridge and continued northeast. After the narrow 217 bike path bridge, we took the muddy dirt trail along the north side of the Atascadero Creek until just shy of Ward Dr. We headed north to the bike trail and walked west and south on the bike trail, eventually returning to our car. Our first time birding this location (we weren't sure how most birders cover this area and meandered a bit - it was fun). Later, I realized that we covered two hotspots plus non-hotspot territory, but I didn't break up the list while birding and the mileage was low. I changed the hotspot to Atascadero Creek Trail since more species were seen at this location vs. Goleta Slough areas A & H. Track mileage: 2.568. URN:CornellLabOfOrnithology:EBIRD:OBS157941103	2022-12-21 20:24:29.827711	7591	species	avibase-C6772490	Yellow-crowned Night Heron	Nyctanassa violacea				1				Unknown Sex, Adult (1)	United States	US	California	US-CA	Ventura	US-CA-111					Ventura River Estuary	L299264	H	34.2756058	-119.3081546	2008-04-13		obsr57292		S11097710	Historical	Historical	P62						1	0		1	1	1			I chased this bird at the estuary and found it quite easily. It was not seen subsequently. I neglected to keep an ebird checklist though... Date recovered from the CBRC record. Accepted record 2008-056.----CBRC report: --Species: Yellow-crowned Night-Heron, Nyctanassa violacea--Location: Ventura River Mouth, Ventura County.--Date: 13 April 2008--Age and sex: After hatch year, sex unknown--Molt status: None apparent--Number of individuals: 1--Other observers: Eric Waian, two other people I didn’t know--Original observers: Robert and Allison McMorran------Circumstances: I got a message from Robert in the midafternoon of the 13th, after spending all morning hiking, so I raced down to Ventura. Once I got to the Ventura River Mouth I walked out to the river from the Emma Wood State Beach campground, and started walking along the overgrown gravel bar towards the railroad bridge and the river mouth. I didn’t make it 200 feet before a mid-sized dark heron flushed from some reeds along the shore about forty feet in front of me and flew behind me in good light at about twenty foot elevation and headed out to the sand bars at the river mouth. I recognized it as the Yellow-crowned and headed back onto the trails through the willows to get out to the railroad bridge so that I would have a better view of the bird. I ran into Eric on the trails, who hadn’t seen the bird yet, so we both headed out to the bridge, where there were other two birders looking in the wrong direction. The heron was easily visible and we all got good looks through the scope (although a little distant) and I got some decent digiscoped photos. After watching the bird for about fifteen-twenty minutes, I had to leave to return to Santa Barbara. ----Description: A mid-sized dark gray heron, approximately the same size as a Black-crowned Night-Heron (although there were none for direct comparison). The neck and legs were rather short for a heron. In flight the grayish legs extended slightly beyond the short tail. When perched, the tail was mostly hidden by the wings, which were plain gray and slightly darker than the rest of the body. The head was black, fading into the gray of the neck. The crown was white, broad towards the bill, and becoming narrow towards the nape. Another white blaze started just bellow the eye as a narrow point, and became wider as it curved slightly up towards the nape. The bill was very stocky, with a curved culmen, and dark grey. I did not note the eye color.----Discussion: A very distinctive heron. Much smaller than Great Blue, and much larger than Green, the two expected dark herons in the area. Tricolored Heron has a white belly, and Reddish Egret and Little Blue Heron are solidly dark, including on the head. Black-crowned Night-Heron is much paler, and has a black crown, among other characters.

L605251	H	34.0154646	-119.3635561	2025-09-30	15:15:00	obsr263383		S276588013	Traveling	Traveling	P22			14	3.112		1	1		1	1	1			Two juvenile birds near the landing cove.  In the field I assumed Black-crowned but on photo review the structure of the bird was a bit off for Black-crowned. Initially had difficulty discerning which species I was looking at when I reviewed pictures. They were showing small triangular spots on the back and wings with thin white lines but to me this was not the best field mark but was a contributing factor. The spots were sharper looking than the blurry triangular spots on Black-crowned. These birds on Anacapa have a heavier looking bill and more blunt tip than expected on Black-crowned which is also rare for this location. Consulted more experience birders and they confirmed Yellow-crowned Night Heron.  At least one of the birds was standing tall and seemed to have long legs, and a thinner body with a more blocky head. To me Black-crowned seem stockier with a more rounded head into a thicker neck.
